**Surat al-Ra'd**

Its aim is to describe the Book as true in itself. Sometimes it has an effect on people, since it has a sound, a renown, and an awe-inspiring and frightening power that guides in actuality. Sometimes it has no effect, and becomes instead a cause of misguidance and blindness. What best fits this aim in the surah is the thunder (al-Ra'd). Although it is true in itself, it is heard by the blind and the sighted, by what is manifest and what is hidden. Sometimes lightning and rain result from it, and sometimes they do not. When rain falls, it sometimes benefits, when it reaches good land and is free from blight. Sometimes it fails, when it falls on barren salt-flats. Sometimes it harms, through flooding, lightning bolts, hail, and other things. And God knows best.

"In the name of God" (the Truth), besides whom everything is falsehood. "The Most Gracious" (al-Rahman), who encompasses all with both hope and fear through the universality of His mercy. "The Most Merciful" (al-Rahim), who singles out whomever He wills with what He is pleased with, great in His divinity. ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Ra.﴾

When the previous surah concluded with the proof that the Qur'an is true and that it is guidance and mercy for a people who believe, after having pointed to the abundance of His signs that they perceive in the heavens (p-263) and the earth while still turning away, this surah began with that, by way of the figure called *laff wa-nashr* (wrapping and unfolding, i.e., a list followed by its corresponding elements in order), which is disordered, because it is more eloquent for the beginning to unfold with what is closest, then what is next closest. So He said: ﴿Those﴾, that is, the reported news and the clarified narratives, the full moon of meanings, the wondrous wisdoms, the firm foundations and the lofty structures, ﴿are the verses﴾. A verse (*ayah*) is a wondrous indication leading to knowledge, ﴿of the Book﴾ that was sent down to you, and ﴿that﴾ includes all that is "that."

Since it is certain that this Book is from the King, a matter no doubter can approach because of its inimitability, and likewise what follows it of its explanation through the Sunnah, because of its truth which is not hidden from any intelligent person, and since whoever is certain of this will know that the one who brought it can only be great, the verb is put in the passive: ﴿has been sent down to you﴾, being ﴿from your Lord﴾. Thus it became definitively established that it is ﴿the Truth﴾, that is, every part of it is placed in its proper place according to what wisdom calls for, clear, none of it deviating from conformity with reality, whether regarding resurrection or anything else. It is thus farthest from their claim that His promise of resurrection is sorcery. Therefore, for its truth to be established, it is obligatory for everyone endowed with intellect to believe in it. ﴿But most people﴾ (p-264), that is, those who are comfortable with themselves yet restless in their opinions,

﴿do not believe﴾, meaning that no faith at all in its being the Truth in itself and its being from God will emerge from them. Rather, they say it is from Muhammad (ﷺ), and that it is imagination, not something witnessed, as we have said: ﴿And most people, even if you are eager, will not be believers﴾ [Yusuf: 103]. So it is not complete guidance for them, nor perfect mercy. This interpretation is possible. But what is indicated by the apparent sense of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is he who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19] is that *alladhi* ("the one who") is the subject, "from your Lord" is the complement of "has been sent down," and the predicate is "the truth." The purpose of this surah is this verse, namely the description of what was sent down as the truth and the establishing of proof for it. This is because, when the description of the Book as wise, firm, detailed and clear had been completed, the discourse turned to a first detailed elaboration [Surat al-Baqarah]. This also signals that the time had come to gather the fruit in this surah and the one after it, and the description of those who affirm this is joined to it, as you will see.

Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr, may God have mercy on him, said in his *Burhan* (his work on the arrangement of the surahs): This surah is an elaboration of the general statement in the closing of Surat Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by while turning away from it﴾ [Yusuf: 105]; ﴿And most of them do not believe in God except while associating others with Him﴾ [Yusuf: 106]; ﴿Are they then secure from the overwhelming punishment of God (p-265) or the Hour coming upon them suddenly while they perceive not?﴾ [Yusuf: 107]; ﴿Say: This is my way; I invite to God with insight, I and whoever follows me. And glory be to God; and I am not of those who associate others with Him﴾ [Yusuf: 108].

So the explanation of which heavens is in His saying: ﴿God is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you see; then He istawa (established Himself) over the Throne and subjected the sun and the moon, each running to a specified term﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2]. And the explanation of which earth is in His saying: ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth and placed in it firm mountains and rivers, and of all fruits He placed in it two mates, two﴾ [al-Ra'd: 3]. These, then, are the heavens and the earth, and they have been further explained in various places. Then, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ [al-Ra'd: 3], is what comes from the signs in them, because the darkness is from the body of the earth, and the light is from the sun's light, and it is heavenly. Then He, exalted, increased the explanation and elaboration of the earth's signs in His saying: ﴿And in the earth are neighboring tracts﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4], up to His saying: ﴿for a people who reason﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4]. Since bringing forth fruit by the water that descends from the sky is among the greatest of signs, and a clear proof of the validity of the resurrection, for this reason He said in another verse: ﴿Thus do We bring out the dead﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]. Here the greatest aspect for consideration had been presented: bringing forth varieties differing in taste, colors and scents (p-266), while the substance is one, watered with one water, and some of them are preferred over others in eating. Therefore, what follows His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And in the earth are neighboring tracts﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4], the verse, with His saying: ﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying: "When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 5]. Then He, glory be to Him, specified the category who say this, namely the disbelievers, the people of eternal abiding in the Fire. Then He followed that with a great demonstration of His forbearance and pardon, saying: ﴿And they ask you to hasten evil before good﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6], the verse. Then He followed that with what indicates a course in the path of predecessors, in His saying: ﴿You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]. Then He showed the greatness of His dominion and His knowledge of the subtleties of what He brought into existence of His sublime creation and power, saying: ﴿God knows what every female bears and what the wombs diminish and what they increase﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8], the verses, up to His saying: ﴿and they have besides Him no protector﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11]. Then He warned His servants, cautioned them and encouraged them: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as fear and as hope﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12], the verses. All of this refers back to what God, glory be to Him, deposited in the heavens and the earth and what lies between them of signs. And most of the surah is about this. Then He, exalted is He, drew attention to the greatest sign and the supreme miracle, saying: ﴿If only a Qur'an by which mountains were set in motion, or the earth were split asunder, or the dead were made to speak...﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. The meaning is: then this Qur'an would have been [such a sign]. ﴿And had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ [al-Nisa': 82]. The admonition by means of this great sign (p-267) is appropriate to the requirement of the surah, which is to admonish by what God, exalted is He, deposited of signs in the heavens and the earth. It is as if He, majestic and exalted, when He had shown them the greatness of what He deposited in the heavens and the earth and what lies between them of signs, and had expanded and clarified that, followed it with another verse comprehensive of the signs and broad for considerations, saying, exalted is He:

﴿If only a Qur'an by which mountains were set in motion﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. It is of the same kind as: ﴿Indeed, in the heavens and the earth are signs for the believers﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 3], ﴿and in your own creation﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 4]. That is: if you reflect on the signs of the heavens and the earth, they would suffice you and be enough for you in indicating the way to Him. And if you reflect on yourselves and what God, exalted is He, deposited in you of wonders, you would be satisfied: "Whoever knows himself knows his Lord." So this kind of consideration is what occurs in Surat al-Ra'd, in the expansion of the signs of the heavens and the earth, then the mention of the Qur'an and what it contains. This is an allusion to what this glorious surah includes of expanding upon the signs deposited in the earths and the heavens.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God except while associating others with Him﴾ [Yusuf: 106], it is alluded to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But most people do not believe﴾ [al-Ra'd: 1], and: ﴿Only those of understanding remember﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of God. Verily, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28]. Those whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of God (p-268) are the people of understanding who remember, the perfect in faith, and they are the few alluded to in His saying: ﴿And few are they﴾ [Sad: 24], of whom it is said: ﴿Those are the true believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 4]. Below these are groups of believers who are not at their level and have not attained their certainty, and to them is the allusion in His saying: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God except while associating others with Him﴾ [Yusuf: 106]. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Shirk in my community is more hidden than the crawling of an ant." This is the explanation of what was stated in general in His saying: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God except while associating others with Him﴾ [Yusuf: 106].

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Are they then secure from the overwhelming punishment of God﴾ [Yusuf: 107], what He hastened for them of that is in His saying: ﴿And disaster will not cease to strike those who disbelieve, because of what they have done, or it will settle near their homes, until the promise of God comes﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], which cuts off their root and uproots their affair. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: This is my way; I invite to God with insight﴾ [Yusuf: 108], the verse, Surat al-Ra'd has made clear the way of His peace be upon him, and explained it by what it bore of great admonition, the unfolding of proofs through what is in the heavens and the earth, what lies between them, what is in the whole world, and what the Clear Book contained, as has preceded. Then the surah addresses the clear description of those who travel that clear and saving path, saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who fulfill the covenant of God and do not break the pledge﴾ [al-Ra'd: 20], up to the end of what He adorned them with, in taking and abandoning. Then the discourse returned to what it contains of admonition (p-269) and unfolding, reproof and rebuke of the disbelievers, and consolation for him, peace be upon him, regarding their affair: ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]; ﴿And We had already sent messengers before you and gave them wives and offspring﴾ [al-Ra'd: 38]; ﴿Your duty is only to convey, and Ours is the reckoning﴾ [al-Ra'd: 40]; ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "You are not a messenger"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43]. The surah in its entirety does not deviate from those general aims mentioned in the four verses at the end of Surat Yusuf. Most of the surah and most of its verses are about admonition, unfolding of proofs, and reminder of the greatness of the signs it deposited. Since this is its character, it was followed by the opening of Surat Ibrahim, peace be upon him. End.

When Allah, glory be to Him, established that this Book is distinguished by being the truth, and so it became clear that it is the greatest of proofs and signs, He began to mention what He had alluded to with His words, ﴿And how many a sign﴾ (Yusuf: 105), namely the perceptible, manifest signs. These signs show that the signs of the Book are true, both by their own stability and by what they show of the power and free choice of their Maker. They show that He is able to do all things, that what He has reported of the Resurrection is true because of the wisdom it contains, and they show, through the inimitability of the way they are expressed, that they come from Allah. He began with what He began with among those signs of the heavens because of their nobility and because they are more indicative. So He said: ﴿Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King who alone possesses all the attributes of perfection, ﴿who raised the heavens﴾ after bringing them into existence from non-existence, as you are aware. Raising (rafa') is placing a thing in the direction of height, whether by transport or by origination. [They are raised] ﴿without pillars﴾, the plural of 'imad (pillar), like uhub and ihab, [or 'amud (column). The 'amud is an elongated body that keeps what is raised from tilting, and its root meaning is preventing tilt.] ﴿that you see﴾, that is, visible, bearing these great bodies, which in the ordinary course of your experience cannot be borne by anything of their kind except after a proportion in size. This is on the basis that ﴿that you see﴾ is a descriptive clause. It is also permissible, and perhaps better, that it be understood as an answer to an implied question, as if he had said: What is the proof that they are without pillars? Then it is said: the direct observation, than which nothing is clearer.

[Since the raising of the heavens came after the creation of the earth and before its leveling, He mentioned that He proceeded to] manage what benefits the two worlds and what is in them of accidents and substances. He indicated the greatness of that management by using the particle of delay, so He said: ﴿Then He settled on the Throne﴾. Al-Razi said in Lawami' al-Burhan (Lights of the Proof): "He singled out the Throne because it is the highest of His creation and its choicest part, the place of His supreme vision, the locus of His glorification, the manifestation of His kingship, the origin of His revelation, and the place of His nearness. He did not attribute any of His creation to Himself in the way He attributed this to Himself." So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾ (al-Buruj: 15), just as He said ﴿Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾ (al-Rahman: 27). Dhu (possessor) is a word that indicates right, connection, manifestation and origin. Al-Rummani said: "Istiwa' (settling) is taking control through power and the enforcement of authority. Its root is: the management was made level (istawa al-tadbir), just as the root of qiyam (standing) is erection, and then one says: qa'im bil-tadbir (standing in charge of the management)." End of quotation. He expressed it with thumma (then) because this rank is far from the reach of aspiration and too high for anything attainable, so there is no sequence or interval here that would lead one to understand that what came before was otherwise. The meaning is that He took up the management of what He had created, as is the custom of kings when they settle upon their thrones, that is, no one contests them, even if there is no sitting at all. That is because the spirit of kingship is management, and it is the most just of its conditions. And Allah knows best. ﴿And He subjected﴾, that is, made subservient with a great subjection, ﴿the sun﴾, that is, the one which [is the sign of the day], ﴿and the moon﴾, [that is, the one which] is the sign of the night, because of the wisdoms, benefits and interests contained in them, through which the lands and the servants are made sound. The lam (the article) entered upon both of them, and each of them is unique, because the noun carries the meaning of an attribute. Accordingly, if a like of them were found, one would not hesitate to apply the name to it, which is not the case with Zayd and 'Amr. Taskhir (subjection) is preparing a thing for the purpose for which it is subjected, so that it does this by itself without its owner's labour in what he needs, like the subjection of fire for cooking and of water for flowing. ﴿Each﴾, that is, of the two bodies, ﴿runs﴾.

Since the context concerns management, it is known that their running is for that purpose, which is their movement through the mansions and degrees by which the seasons change, plants vary, and times are regulated. Whenever the management is faster, one knows that its Master is more knowing, especially if He is more wise. Therefore the proper particle here is li (for) and not ila (to). So He gave the cause with His words: ﴿for a term﴾, that is, for the term of a specified time: ﴿appointed﴾. This one's term is a year, and that one's term is a month. A term (ajal) is the time set for the occurrence of a matter and its ending.

Since each of these contains signs that exceed counting, while being in the utmost of firm arrangement, He resumed with a statement that serves as an alert to the wisdom in what has preceded. Having indicated the greatness of this statement through the great attributes in the relative clause (sila), He explained the settling upon the Throne by saying: ﴿He manages the affair﴾, that is, in the livelihood and the afterlife and what orders them, by acting in it as one who looks to its ends and consequences, so that it comes out firm, beyond any attempt to break it. Rather, He is in truth the One who knows the ends and outcomes of affairs. No matter occupies Him from another, even though this world, from the top of the Throne down to what is beneath the soil, contains genera, species, differences, kinds and individuals that none but Him can encompass. This is a definite proof that He, [glory be to Him], in His essence and attributes, is exalted above resemblance to originated things, is One, the Unique, the Eternal Refuge, to whom nothing is equal.

Since this is a great exposition with no ambiguity, He said: ﴿He details the signs﴾, [that is] those whose management has come into existence, which indicate His oneness and perfect wisdom, and which His originated things contain. He distinguishes them and sets them apart with a clarity admitting no confusion, to bring them near to your intellects and to train your understanding, so that you may know that they are the act of the One who chooses, not the act of natures nor of other causes that He originated. Otherwise they would be in a single pattern. He also gathered them, in accordance with the earlier allusion to their multiplicity, in His words: ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth﴾ (Yusuf: 105). It is as if this alif and lam (of the definite article) are for that indefinite there.

Since this management and this detailing indicate complete power and utmost wisdom, and since resurrection, for the final decision and judgment with justice and the manifestation of greatness, is the point to which wisdom leads, He gave the cause with His words: ﴿So that you may, concerning the meeting with your Lord﴾, that is, so that your state be that of one who is hoped to attain, by what he observes of the indications, certainty concerning the meeting with the One who originated him and who is good to him in all that his upbringing requires, ﴿be certain﴾, that is, you know this without doubt, by inferring from the power to originate creation the power over what custom holds to be easier than origination, namely re-creation, and that wisdom is not complete except by it.

When al-Biqa'i had finished with what he intended regarding the signs of the heavens, he followed it with what he had repeated in the verse of Yusuf, among the proofs. He said: ﴿And He﴾, that is, alone, ﴿is the One who spread out the earth﴾. Had He willed, He would have made it like a wall or a vault on which no one could find a settled place. This does not contradict that it is a sphere, because when a sphere is very large, every part of it is seen as a flat surface, just as the mountains are pegs and animals settle upon it. ﴿And He placed in it﴾ mountains, along with their peaks, ﴿firmly fixed mountains (rawasi)﴾, that is, immovable ones. The singular is rasiyah, meaning fixed and enduring in its place, not moving from its locations, not shifting, so that what it is fixed in does not move. Since the word was dominated by its use for mountains and was described as "rawasi," the adjective came to stand in place of the noun, so it was pluralized like a noun, as in ḥā'iṭ (wall) and kāhil (shoulder). This was said by Abu Hayyan. Since the nature of the earth is one, the presence of a mountain in one part of it and not another, and the existence in it of different minerals, sometimes gems, sometimes metals, sometimes petroleum, sometimes sulfur, and other things, are evidence that Almighty God alone has complete power and choice, because the mountain is one in its nature, just as the influence of the sun is one. So He, Exalted, said: ﴿And rivers﴾, that is, and He placed in it rivers flowing out [from it]. Most rivers come from mountains, because mountains are hard, high bodies, and within the earth there are vapors. These vapors that form in the depths of the earth rise and keep breaking through until they reach the mountains, where they are held back, and they continue to accumulate until their condensation becomes great. When they cool, they turn into water, and so much water comes about through them, just as the vapors condensed in the upper parts of bathhouses cool and drip. When the formation of this water is complete and it has grown large, it splits the lower parts of the mountains or other places that are weak against its strength and the strength of the vapors accompanying it. If that water has a continual supply from the active and receptive causes, so that whenever something springs from it, something else arises after it, and so on continuously, then it is a "nahr" (river). The nahr is a wide course among the channels of water, and its root meaning is expansion; from it comes nahar (day), because its light expands.

When He mentioned the rivers, He mentioned what grows from waters. He said: ﴿And of all the fruits﴾. It is possible that this is connected to what comes before, and then it would be as if it were said: who benefits from these things? So it was said: ﴿He placed in it﴾, that is, in the earth, ﴿two pairs﴾, a male and a female, of every kind of living creature that benefits from it. It is also possible that it is connected to what follows, and then the meaning would be: and He placed in it, of all the fruits, two pairs, a male and a female, so that the female benefits from its fertilization by the male or its being brought near to it, and so its fruit becomes good. The fruit is the food of the tree. The zawj (pair) is a form that has a companion, either a counterpart or an opposite. So it is as if it were said: what is it that ripens them? He said: ﴿He covers the night with the day﴾, that is, and the day the night, so that this one ripens by its heat and that one holds back by its cold. Their actions are balanced according to what God, Exalted, has determined for them in their courses, in increase and decrease, for heat and cold, for bringing forth and ripening, and other wise purposes that benefit religion and worldly life, which are evident to everyone of intellect: that they are by His arrangement, by His act, by His choice, by His dominion, and by His power.

When He, Glorified is He, presented these signs in detail, dividing them into four, and there was in them subtlety, He gathered them together and linked them to reflection, saying: ﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, in what has been described of signs, linked together, ﴿are signs﴾, that is, clear, wondrous, dazzling proofs that all of this is grounded in His power and choice. He drew attention to the fact that this situation requires effort, by stripping the soul of desire and purely applying the intellect, through His saying: ﴿for a people﴾, that is, people who have strength beyond standing firm in what they attempt, ﴿who reflect﴾, that is, who exert themselves in thinking. Al-Rummani said: it is the turning of the heart in seeking meaning, and its beginning is a meaning that God, Exalted, places in the mind of a person, so he seeks its connections, in which there is an explanation of it from every aspect possible. Ending with reflection indicates attention to giving this situation its due in refuting the philosophers, for they attribute the events of the lower world to the differing configurations of the stars. This is a baseless claim for anyone who reflects on what He, Glorified is He, established in the previous verse, namely that it is He who brought all things into existence from nothing and then began to arrange them. So the specialization of each [thing] of the heavenly bodies with a nature, quality, and property is only by the specification of the wise, active, choosing Manager, so that the existence of lower events, even if it were granted that they are affected by upper events, is ascribed to them only in terms of causation, and the cause and the effect are ascribed to the eternal Creator, the wise Manager.

(p-279) When the proof, despite its clarity, contains some obscurity, the Exalted began to detail some of the signs on the earth that are clearer than that and are a very manifest proof against the claim of the philosophers (al-falasifa, the Greek-influenced philosophers). So He said: ﴿And on the earth﴾, that is, the earth in which you dwell, where you witness what is in it with a witnessing that admits no doubt, ﴿are neighboring tracts﴾. They share one piece of ground but differ in nature: good soil adjoins salt-flat soil, fertile soil adjoins barren soil, hard soil adjoins soft soil, and some soil suits crops but not trees, or the reverse. Despite all of these being included in the category of earth, ﴿and gardens﴾, plural of jannah, which is an orchard whose trees cover the ground, ﴿of grapes﴾. It seems He mentioned them first because their varieties, which testify that their Maker is the One who does what He wills, cannot be counted. Even from a single root, the fruit can vary.

Since the variation of what originates from the grain is more striking, He said: ﴿and cultivated plants﴾, that is, (p-279) standing alone, in the reading of Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hafs from 'Asim with the nominative (raf'), and within the gardens, in the reading of the rest with the genitive (jarr).

Since what a single root produces is more evident, yet more remarkable in its diversity, He placed after it: ﴿and palm trees, some multiple-stemmed and some single-stemmed﴾. Ṣinwān refers to branches spreading from one root, and ghayr ṣinwān refers to those whose roots and origins are separate. Abu Hayyan said: "al-ṣinw is a branch that joins with another from one root, and its origin is the likeness (mathal). From it comes the saying for a paternal uncle, ṣinw." Al-Rummani said: "al-ṣinwān are those that are closely joined; one says, 'He is the son of his brother [ṣinw abihi]', meaning his father's close relative by birth. It is the plural of ṣinw." It was also said: "al-ṣinwān are the palm shoots whose root is one." This is related from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, may Allah be pleased with them. Al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "al-ṣinwān are two palms whose root is one." End of quotation.

This is a construction in which there is no difference between its dual and its plural except that the nun is written with a kasra without tanwin, and its declension is with tanwin. The secret of calling the vine "ʿinab" (grape) will come in Surah Yasin, if Allah the Exalted wills.

Since water stands in the position of the father and the earth in the position of the mother, and since variation despite the unity of father and mother is more remarkable and more indicative of attribution to the One who originates and causes, and not to any of the causes, He said: ﴿watered﴾ [al-Ghashiya: 5], that is, its one earth in its entirety (p-280) ﴿with one water﴾. Then its branches and fruits come forth at a known time that neither lags behind nor precedes it, after the water has risen up within them, contrary to its natural tendency to descend, and then it spreads into each of the leaves, branches and fruits in the measure of what suits their well-being. ﴿And We make some of them excel﴾, that is, by Our greatness, which requires obedience, ﴿some of them﴾, that is, some of those gardens and some of their trees, ﴿over others﴾. Since excellence takes various forms, He clarified the intended meaning with His words: ﴿in fruit﴾, that is, the eatable fruit, which differs in taste although the land and some of the roots are the same. Eating was singled out because it is the most common way of benefiting, and it points to the difference in other respects such as fiber, palm fronds, color of what is eaten, taste, nature, shape, smell, benefit and others. Moreover, the relation of the natures and the celestial influences to all fruits is equal, especially when you see one cluster in which all the grapes are sweet, ripe and large except for one, which is sour, small and dry.

Since the intended meaning in this context, as already stated, is the detailing of what He indicated the multitude of with His words: ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Yusuf: 105], He said: ﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, the great matter that has preceded, ﴿are signs﴾, in the plural form, since, considering its details joined by conjunction, it is plural, although, considering the water, it is singular. This differs from (p-281) what comes in al-Nahl, because the subject spoken of there is the water, while here it is what arises from it. Since the subject spoken of differs, the discourse follows it. The meaning is: clear indications that all of that is one act of a chooser, knowing and capable, who does what He wills, from the beginning of creation and then its diversification after its origination. Thus He is capable of restoring it, all the more so.

Since these detailed signs are more manifest than those mentioned in general terms, and so are clear to the point that the one who considers them needs nothing but reason to reflect upon them, He said: ﴿for a people﴾, that is, those possessing strength to grasp what they seek, ﴿who reason﴾. The expression of this indication cannot be otherwise than by saying that these lower events came into being without a cause that brought them into existence. It is said to the one who says this: "You have no intellect, for knowledge that the originated needs an originator is necessary, so lacking knowledge of what is necessary entails the lack of intellect."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 5:

When it was established, in pieces, by the proof He set forth of His great power, through the marvels He deposited in His dominion, which none other than He can accomplish, that this is nothing but one act, dominating and choosing, which brings the non-existent into being and differentiates between things whose natures would require them to be uniform, denying any part of His power became a matter of wonder. So He said, conjoining it to His saying ﴿But most of the people do not believe﴾ [al-Ra'd: 1], indicating that they say: the promise of resurrection is sorcery with no reality. ﴿And if you are amazed﴾, that is, on any day of the days or any hour of time, then be amazed at (p-282) their denial of resurrection ﴿—then amazing is﴾ great, whose degrees of greatness are endless, ﴿their saying﴾ after they had seen the dazzling signs and the clear indications of His great power over everything, denying: ﴿"When we are dust?"﴾ And the dust into which we are turned has mixed with the original dust so that it cannot be distinguished. Then they repeated the amazement and denial by way of interrogation a second time, saying: ﴿"Are we indeed in a new creation?"﴾ This is their saying after We had detailed from the signs what necessitates that they are certain of meeting their Lord. This second interrogation explains what the first one was governed by, through the meaning in it, "will we be raised" (anbu'atha). Al-'ajab (wonder): the change of the soul by something whose cause is hidden from its habit. Al-jadid (new): that which is prepared, by cutting off, for formation before being put to use in works; and the root of the attribute is cutting (al-qat'). Al-Rummani said: It has been said: there is no good in one who does not marvel at what is marvelous, and more contemptible than him is one who marvels at what is not marvelous. That is, the disbelievers marvelled at what was not marvelous; and whoever marvels at them has marvelled at the marvelous.

Since this denial concerns what is perceptible of His power, they deserved what one deserves who disparages the King of kingdoms. So He said: ﴿Those﴾, that is, those who have gathered kinds of distance together with every good ﴿are those who disbelieved in their Lord﴾, that is, they covered over everything that must be made manifest, through contempt for the One who began their creation and then nurtured them with kinds of gentleness. So when they deny their return, they have denied their origin. ﴿And those﴾ [that is] the distant, the hated ﴿—the shackles﴾, that is, the iron rings that gather the hands of captives to their necks; they are also called "jawami'" (collars). Sometimes they are only on the necks, with which people are tormented. Since the two sides of the neck are thick, the collar cannot encompass them when it is tight except at the middle; so He made the necks like containers, in view of their being upon some of it, and that is a metaphor for their narrowness. So He said: ﴿on their necks﴾, that is, because of their disbelief, even though the shackles are not visible now; they are, by the capability of the one threatened with them to act, as though they were existing, and they are led by what He has determined upon them of its causes, just as the shackled one is led wherever his leader wishes. Al-ghill: a collar by which the hand is fettered at the neck; its root is "insalla fi al-shay'" (to become entangled in a thing) when it is caught in it, and "ghalla al-mal" (to embezzle) when one betrays by being entangled in unlawful property. ﴿And those﴾, that is, those for whom no loss is greater than their loss ﴿are the companions of the Fire﴾. Since companionship entails constancy, He stated it explicitly, saying: ﴿they﴾, that is, exclusively ﴿therein﴾, that is, purely, with no bliss mixed into it ﴿abide forever﴾, that is, their eternity is firmly established, perpetually.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 6:

Since this verse contains the affirmation of complete power, together with the visible and observable proofs that preceded it, it is also a wondrous marvel and a strange matter that they mock it. So He says, expressing wonder at them: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil﴾, i.e., in mockery and denial. Al-isti'jal (hastening) is seeking to make something come early, which is bringing a thing before its appointed time. ﴿With evil﴾, meaning the punishment threatened to them, both the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, is an act of audacity on their part, indicating that they do not care about any of it and that nothing weakens their claim. ﴿Before the good﴾, meaning the good that you announce to them, ﴿while﴾ the situation is that ﴿there have already passed away﴾. Since the one spoken of was only in some period of time, the preposition was introduced, and He said: ﴿Before them, the exemplary punishments (al-mathulat)﴾, the plural of mathulah, with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the tha' [like sadaqah and sadaqat; it was named so because of the equivalence between the punishment and what is punished for]. These are the punishments that deter from the like of what befell the nations for whose sake they came, the nations whose reports reached them, and whose traces and dwellings addressed them with the great things that befell them. And Allah only delays them in order to fulfil their appointed terms, which He set for them, along with His complete power over them.

Since they might say: "We see nothing but a threat, none of which will come to pass," He said, emphasising the refutation of them and their belief that gain and harm are merely the custom of time, by way of conjunction with what is implied: "Indeed your Lord is forbearing and does not fear escape, so He does not hasten in seizing": ﴿And indeed your Lord﴾, i.e., the one who is good to you by making you a prophet of mercy, ﴿is certainly Possessor of forgiveness﴾ (p-285), i.e., great and enduring, ﴿for the people﴾ while they are ﴿wrongdoers, firmly established in wrongdoing, independent in their wrongdoing﴾, which is their placing things other than in their proper places. So He does not take them to account for all that they earn [﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to account for what they have earned, He would not leave upon the earth a single creature﴾ (Fatir: 45)]. Therefore people remain a long time disbelieving and are not punished, out of His forbearance, glorified is He. The verse is restricted by the verse of an-Nisa': ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (an-Nisa': 48), even if it is not repentance, for the penitent is not upon his wrongdoing.

Since He, glorified is He, gives respite and does not neglect, [and] He mentioned His respite, He mentioned His seizing, emphasising the like of what has passed, and so He said: ﴿And indeed your Lord﴾, i.e., the one who brought you into being and manages your affair with utmost goodness, ﴿is severe in punishment﴾ against the disbelievers and whomever else He wills among others. Therefore He seizes with the seizing of the Mighty, the All-Powerful, when the appointed term He has decreed comes.

When God Most High had explained that they had covered over the signs of their Lord, who had shown them favour through those signs and others, He marvelled at them in another respect: their demand that signs be sent down, even though signs are equal in their indication of the Maker and of what He possesses of attributes of perfection. Since they disbelieved in what had already come to them, they were deserving of disbelief in what would come to them. So He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why is a sign not sent down upon him from his Lord?"﴾ That is, on a continuous basis, ﴿those who disbelieve﴾, mocking at the power [of God]. ﴿Why not﴾ means: why would it not be so, why not? ﴿Sent down﴾ means: by the sending down of whatever being it may be. ﴿Upon him a sign﴾ (p. 286), denying out of obstinacy what he had received of the signs ﴿from his Lord﴾, that is, the One who did good to him, as a confirmation of him.

Since the Prophet (ﷺ) was eager to answer their proposals, because of his intense concern for their faith, it was as if he had asked for this so that they might attain salvation. He was answered with His saying, may He be exalted, placing first what the context gives priority to, because it is to explain that most people do not believe: ﴿You are only a warner﴾, that is, a prophet who warns and guides them, guiding them by explaining what He has sent down to you of what casts into destruction or leads to salvation, proceeding among them according to what He has determined for you. The root of *indhār* (warning) is informing about the place of fear [*li-yuttaqā*, so that one may guard against it], not that you establish faith in the hearts. ﴿And for every people﴾ among those to whom We sent a prophet ﴿is a guide﴾, that is, a caller who guides them to their right path, and a warner who warns them against their pitfalls. That is, he explains to them what We sent him with, of warning and good tidings. And We gave every warner and guide signs fitting to him and to his people, by the like of which humans believe. So God guides whoever He knows to have the capacity for guidance through the visible signs He has set up, and so he needs none of the proposals. And whoever He knows [to have in him] the motives for misguidance goes astray even if every sign came to him, because He is the One who fashioned them with the natures of good and evil (p. 287). ﴿Does not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk: 14]. This is like His saying: ﴿And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾ [Fatir: 24], and like His saying in this surah: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why is a sign not sent down upon him from his Lord?" Say: "Indeed, God misguides whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27].

The verse is an instance of *iḥtibāk* (a rhetorical device in which mention of one term implies the omission of its counterpart): mention of the warner first indicates the omission of the guide second, and mention of the guide second indicates the omission of the like of it first.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 8:

When what has preceded was ordered upon knowledge and power, especially as He concluded this verse with "guide" (hadin), and their denial of resurrection was a denial of the first creation, and Glorified and Exalted is He knew that granting them what they proposed would not benefit them, because they were obstinate seekers of trouble and not seekers of guidance, He—glorified be He, after turning away from answering their proposals—began to establish, from His sensible acts that are visible to them, acts that necessitate His attributes of knowledge and power and that are like the restoration (al-i'adah), whether as an indication from Him, exalted is He, that [if] the denial of resurrection [is] because restoration is impossible, then it is like the originating (al-bada'ah); and if it is because it is impossible to distinguish the dust from which the animal was created after it has been mixed with other things and its parts scattered, then distinguishing the water from which the child comes from the water that is not suitable for that is more remarkable, because water is more thoroughly mixed and its blending is more hidden. Yet He knows it. So He said: ﴿Allah﴾, that is, the One who encompasses everything in knowledge and power, ﴿knows﴾, that is, with eternal knowledge in the pre-eternity of what will come into existence, and with a knowledge whose relation renews according to the occurrence of events continually, ﴿what every female bears﴾, that is, what she carries in her womb, ﴿every female﴾, that is, the water that is suitable to become a fetus, ﴿and what the wombs diminish﴾, that is, decrease, ﴿of water﴾, so that it absorbs it and it perishes because it is not fit to become a child from it. The root of gheed (diminishing), as al-Rummani said, is the going of a liquid into a deep hollow; its verb is transitive and intransitive. ﴿And what they increase﴾, that is, what the wombs add of water beyond the water which God, exalted is He, has decreed to be a fetus, so that it becomes twins or more in another intercourse after the first pregnancy—as Ibn Sina and other physicians have affirmed the possibility of this, and in our time a she-ass gave birth to a donkey and a mule. [This is because] increase is the addition of something to a quantity and its multiplication, one thing after another; He determines that, and no one can increase it or decrease it. All of this necessitates wisdom. Therefore He concluded it with His saying: ﴿And everything﴾, that is, of this and other than it, of the proposed signs and others, ﴿with Him﴾, that is, in His power and knowledge, ﴿is in measure﴾, in its quality and quantity, not exceeding it nor falling short of it, because He knows the quality and quantity of everything in the detailed and clear manner, so confusion in those known things is impossible, while He [is able] to do what He wills with them. Thus the verse is an explanation of His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve in their Lord﴾ [al-Ra'd: 5], in that it clarifies [in it] His nurturing of them in the manner they witness and acknowledge.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 13, verse 9:**

Since this (concealment) is a defect, and His knowledge of it entails knowledge of the observable, and since explicitness has a merit that cannot be hidden, He stated it explicitly in a universal form that encompasses those particulars and others. So He said: ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾, which is what is hidden from every creature, ﴿and the visible﴾. Al-Rummani said: the unseen is the state of a thing being such that it is concealed from the senses, and the visible is the state of a thing being such that it is manifest to Him.

Since knowledge and wisdom are not complete except with perfect power and greatness, He said: ﴿the Great﴾ [i.e.] the One before whom everything that has attributes requiring greatness shrinks. Imam Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali said: Greatness (al-kibr) is the manifestation of disparity in an apparent and dazzling measure that does not need reflection. For this reason it is an innate disposition (fitrah) in creation that God is greatest. Since creatures have no apparent measure of worth, because of the obvious necessities and manifest needs upon them, which are small in worth, and whoever among them tries to become great through force, domination, or corruption, his littleness increases by what he has acquired in the eyes of the people of insight in this world. This appears from him to the eyes of all creation in the Hereafter: "The arrogant will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection like ants, trampled upon by people with their feet." Therefore the meaning that there is no Great but God is specific to Him, and so ends his words.

﴿the Exalted﴾ [i.e.] the One who is not approached, from the peak of His loftiness, in essence, attribute, or act, by any exalted one. He expressed it in the form of reciprocity (tafa'ul) so that it would be more indicative of the meaning and more emphatic in it. Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali, may God have mercy on him, said: Ta'ali (exaltation) is the escape from being reached or attained by proof or argument, and the form of reciprocity indicates what occurs through the imaginings of those who argue about His matter with false, baseless proofs: ﴿Their argument is baseless in the sight of their Lord﴾ [al-Shura: 16]. He, exalted is He, permits argument and disputation, then exalts Himself by the conclusive proof He possesses: ﴿Say: To God belongs the conclusive proof﴾ [al-An'am: 149]. So He is the Exalted in knowledge, judgment, and proof, and the reality of the Exalted is the One who does not exalt Himself except Him, and so ends his words. The summary is that when He described Himself with what preceded, He indicated that this is according to what the intellects can bear, and that the truth in describing Him is absolute greatness and absolute exaltation, because intellects cannot bear more than that.

When custom dictates that knowledge varies with respect to the secret and the open, and power varies with respect to one who is protected by guards and others, He, glorified is He, followed this with what negates that possibility, by way of explanation and clarification, since the unseen and the witnessed are equal with respect to His knowledge. So He said: ﴿Whether among you is one who conceals the speech﴾, i.e., its meaning hidden within himself, ﴿or one who speaks it aloud﴾ and [is manifest] in His knowledge and (p-291) His power, ﴿one who hides himself﴾, i.e., one who brings about concealment and seeks it with the utmost effort, ﴿by night﴾, in the most hidden of times, so he is one who hides or lurks in it, thinking that such concealment will spare him from [divine] power; ﴿and one who goes about freely﴾, i.e., one who goes on his way upon the earth, proceeding swiftly toward his aim, ﴿by day﴾, openly displaying his going about in it. This verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which two terms are mentioned, each one implying the opposite or the like of the other): he mentioned ﴿hides himself﴾ first, which implies its opposite second, and he mentioned "goes about freely" second, which implies its opposite or its like first.

﴿لَهُ﴾ means "for that person" (that is, the one who hides himself or goes about openly by night), as Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said. ﴿مُعَقِّباتٌ﴾ means "successive (guardians)," that is, helpers and supporters who take turns in his affair, each one [replacing] his companion and standing in for him.

Since guarding the front and the back implies guarding the right and the left, and it is impossible for the guardians to fill every one of these directions around a created being, the verse says, with the preposition expressed: ﴿مِن بَيْنِ يَدَيْهِ﴾ "from before him" (that is, from his front) ﴿وَمِن خَلْفِهِ﴾ "and from behind him." Then it resumes explaining the benefit of the successive guardians and says: ﴿يَحْفَظُونَهُ﴾ "they guard him" (that is, in his own supposition) from everything he fears ﴿مِنْ أَمْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ "by the command of Allah," the One who possesses complete encompassing power.

Since this indicates the utmost power, and it is the custom of powerful kings of the earth to encroach upon their neighbours, seize their dominions and oppress them, in order to increase their means and expand their realm, especially when such a neighbour, despite his weakness and incapacity, supposes that some barrier will protect him from their seizure, the Exalted informed [the one] who seemed to ask about this that He had changed this [state of affairs] for the sake of His self-sufficiency from it, saying: ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوْمٍ حَتَّى يُغَيِّرُوا مَا بِأَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ "Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves." Here "Allah" means the One who possesses all encompassing and perfection; ﴿مَا بِقَوْمٍ﴾ means the condition of a people, whether good or bad; ﴿مَا بِأَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ means what is in themselves, from the things they adorn themselves with, such as adopting righteous deeds and abandoning the characteristics of corrupters. When they change that, He changes what is upon them if He wills, even if they are at the height of strength.

Since the kings of this world are generally unable to achieve all their desires, because of the many opponents among those who are similarly qualified for kingship, the Exalted said, linking [this] to what is implied by the context (meaning: when they change what is in themselves, He sends evil upon them): ﴿وَإِذَا أَرَادَ اللَّهُ بِقَوْمٍ سُوءًا فَلا مَرَدَّ لَهُ﴾ "And when Allah wills evil for a people, there is no turning it back," meaning that Allah, who possesses the attributes of perfection, when He wills evil for a people, even if they are at the height of strength, there is no one who can avert it from Him other than Him. This verse has already received further explanation in Surat al-Anfal.

Since every individual is inferior to Him in rank, and none can possibly take His place in any way, He said: ﴿وَمَا لَهُمْ﴾ "and they have not," and He clarified that all ranks are lowly compared to His rank, so He said: "from beside Him" (min dūnihi), and He intensified the negation, [saying]: ﴿مِن﴾ "any." Since the context clearly indicates that they have no escape from what He wills, He used the form of the defective active participle (wāl, "a protector"), as an indication of the negation of even the lowest aspect of guardianship, let alone what is above it. So He said: ﴿وَالٍ﴾ "any protector," meaning [any] refuge that would shelter them, given that the action taken with them, in terms of deliverance and support, is like what a close relative does for his nearest guardian.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 12:

Then He (Exalted is He) informed of a matter which is the proof of what precedes it, encompassing knowledge and power, and it is more subtle than all of that, indicating the magnificence of power in that when He wills evil, there is no repelling it; and the subtlety of wisdom, because it is a single manifestation from which blessing is hoped for and retribution is feared. So He said: ﴿He it is who shows you﴾, that is, He alone, ﴿who shows you﴾ [that is -] in a manner of continual renewal at all times, ﴿the lightning﴾, which is a flash like a pillar of fire, ﴿as a fear﴾, that is, for the sake of the intention of fear of His power to make it destructive thunderbolts. Fear is the agitation of the soul through imagining the occurrence of harm.

Since they had no causal role in sending down the rain, He did not express it with hope, and said: (p-294) ﴿and as a hope﴾, that is, and for the sake of the intention of your hope for His mercy, that it may be beneficial rain. This estimate is necessary so that both would be the act of the agent of the caused act. It is also permissible that the meaning is: He shows you that as a means of frightening and encouraging, so that you fear with fear and hope with hope. Then the verse is of the ihtiba' (interlocking) type: the verb of showing indicates frightening and encouraging, and "fear" and "hope" indicate "you fear and you hope." It is also permissible that both are circumstantial accusatives from the pronoun of the addressees, meaning those possessing fear and hope. ﴿And He produces﴾; and al-inshа' (production) is the making of a thing without a generating cause; ﴿the clouds﴾, which are the gathering clouds drawn along in the sky, and it is a collective noun of genus whose singular is saḥābah; ﴿the heavy﴾, laden with rivers of water carried in the air upon the back of the wind; and heaviness (thiql) is reliance on the direction of weight through the density of its parts.

﴿And the thunder glorifies Him﴾, that is, it declares Him far above deficient attributes, with a glorification joined to ﴿His praise﴾, that is, by ascribing to Him the attributes of perfection. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that the thunder is an angel [and even if it is not established that it is an angel, its glorification is its indication that its Originator, glory be to Him, is exalted above deficiency, encompassing the attributes of perfection]. ﴿And the angels﴾, that is, they glorify Him ﴿out of awe of Him﴾. Al-Rummani said: "The word khīfah (awe) is construed as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), as when you say, 'This is a fine rukbah (riding manner),' meaning a fine state of riding. Likewise, 'This is a severe khīfah,' whereas khawf (fear) is a verbal noun that is not construed as a circumstantial state."

﴿And He sends the thunderbolts﴾, the burning ones, from those clouds laden with waters that drown. The ṣāʿiqah (thunderbolt): al-Razi said it is a subtle fire that falls from the sky in a terrifying state.

﴿So He strikes with them﴾, that is, with the thunderbolts, ﴿whom He wills﴾, just as it struck Arbad ibn Rabi'ah. ﴿Yet they﴾, that is, while they, despite what has preceded of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and the perfection of His power, ﴿dispute﴾. Jidal (disputation) is turning an opponent away from his position by means of argument, ﴿concerning God﴾, that is, the Supreme King, in a manner that leads to doubt [concerning] His power and knowledge. And since nothing avails one whom He intends with punishment, He says: ﴿and He is mighty in strength (shadīd al-miḥāl)﴾, because al-miḥāl, like kitāb (book), means: cunning, contriving affairs through stratagems, planning, deception, power, disputation, punishment and retribution, enmity and hostility, strength and might, destruction and annihilation. He brings upon His enemies what He wills of descending punishment upon them from where they do not reckon, and all of these are apt [here] in the literal or the figurative sense. Al-Rummani said: "al-miḥāl" is the seizing of punishment, from their saying, 'I maḥaltu fulānan,' when I drew him toward his destruction." End of quotation.

The root "m-ḥ-l" in all its permutations revolves around turning a thing away from its face, its customary course, and what its nature requires. That entails power, strength and might. Thus the bearer holds the borne by his strength from falling downward. The ḥamlah is a charge in war. Carrying entails hardship. From it comes taḥammala (to bear) and ḥumila ʿanhu (to be borne on his behalf), i.e., he was forbearing (ḥalama), so he is ḥamūl, possessing ḥilm (forbearance). The ḥamīl (adopted one or stranger) is, like amīr, one who is a claimed child or a stranger, as if both are carried because of their need for that. And the kafīl (guarantor) is one who carries every person under guarantee. And iḥtamala lawnahu (he bore its color), in the passive, meaning: he became angry and turned pale, as if anger turned him away from his customary state. The maḥmal (litter, or a woman whose milk flows without pregnancy) is, like muḥsin, a woman whose milk descends without conception, because that is a thing contrary to its proper course. The ḥamal, with vowels ḥamal, is a lamb, because of the ease of carrying it. The ḥalīm is one who restrains his anger by the strength of his ḥilm, that is, his intellect, from being swayed by anger. Ḥilm with a kasra means deliberation and intellect. Ḥulm with a damma or two dammas means a dream, because it turns the soul away from what it is upon, and that is the nature of heedlessness. From it comes ḥulm (with damma) and iḥtilām, the nocturnal emission during sleep. The noun ḥulm, like ʿunuq, occurs mostly when the mind is free of cares, and to it returns ḥulm al-māl (the fatness of wealth) with a damma: fat. A child or other one's fat grows plentiful. Or it derives from ḥalamah, with vowels, meaning the protruding flesh at the center of the breast like a wart, because it turns the color and shape of the breast from what they were. Shajar al-saʿdān (saʿdān plant) is so named because it is good pasture that fattens livestock. The small or large tick is so named for its resemblance to the nipple of the breast, and a worm that falls into the hide before tanning and eats it, because that alters it from its form. The ḥālūm is a kind of curd, because by its sharpness it changes the tongue. Dam ḥulām means wasted blood, because it came out contrary to the customary course of blood. Salt turns what is salted away from corruption. As for salty water, it is likened to it in taste. Likewise milḥ (with fatḥah on the miim and sukūn on the lām) for a color like whiteness mixed with blackness. The malḥāʾ is a tree whose leaves have fallen, likened to salt land in not producing growth. Since salt is known for goodness, knowledge was likened to it and named milḥ. Likewise suckling, beauty, fat, grease, sanctity, protection, and the fluttering of a bird with its wings, by which its flight is made good; one seeks sweetness through it, seeking comfort in it. Mallaḥa al-shāh means he skewered the sheep. The mallāḥ, like kitāb, is a wind by which the ship runs, and it too turns it from what its state requires of not moving, and from treating the she-camel's shyness toward it. "Milḥuhu ʿalā rukbatihi" means he has no fidelity, because salt does not hold there, or it means he is fat or hard in his anger, in the sense that there is no good in him. Malaḥahu means he backbit him, likened to one who eats salt to balance his temperament. Likewise al-mallāḥ, like kitāb, is the south wind blowing after the north. Likewise al-milāḥī, like farābī and sometimes with shaddah, is a long white grape, a kind of fig, and of the arāk tree that which has whiteness and redness. Al-mulaḥ, with a damma on the miim and fatḥah on the lām, means fabrications in narrations. Imtalaḥa means he mixed falsehood with truth. Al-milḥ, with fatḥah, is a swelling in the hock of a horse, which turned it from its customary form. Al-milāḥ, like kitāb, is the point of the spear, because it prepares it for penetration after standing; and a screen, because it turns sight from passing through to what is behind it. And the coolness of the earth when rain descends, because it turns its state from what it was to another. Al-mulḥah, with a damma, is awe, because it turns the bold one from his intent; and because its cause turns the soul from its desire. Al-malḥāʾ is the great dune, and from it comes blessing, because it hinders the walker from his manner of walking. From it also comes al-malḥah, with fatḥah, the depth of the sea. Milḥān is January, because by the strength of its cold it turns time from what it was, and people from what they were. Al-malḥāʾ is flesh on the spine from the shoulder blade to the buttocks, because it prevents seeing the bones of the spine and the heads of the ribs. Al-maḥall is turning what is in time from its customary course by lack of rain and vegetation and by ease of living. Likewise al-maḥall means deceit, guile, dust, severity and places of alighting, for what has preceded in its explanation. From it: māḥalahu means he contended with him. Al-mutamāḥil is the tall, restless-tempered one, because he departed from custom. Tamaḥḥala lahu means he schemed. Al-mumaḥḥal, like muʿaẓẓam, of milk is that which takes on a sourness in taste. Al-mimḥalah is the great pulley, because by turning it turns the thing from its face. Al-faqrah is from faqara al-baʿīr (the camel's vertebra), because of its resemblance; and the plank on which the builders stand, because it bears them and keeps them from falling. Al-maḥal, like kataf, is one who has been driven away until he is exhausted, because he was turned from what was his customary course. And you see him mutamāḥḥil, changed in color. Al-laḥm is the turning of sight from what it was. The lamḥ of lightning is its shining after it was hidden. Al-laḥm, from the weft of cloth, with a damma, as if it closes the gap produced by thinness. From it: laḥama kulla shayʾin means he made every thing its core. Laḥama al-amr, like manaʿa, means he made it firm. The goldsmith solders silver with its mother, and likewise every crack. Laḥima, like ʿilm, means he settled in the place, as if he fell into something resembling flesh and stuck to it, entangling and occupying him. "This is the laḥīm of that" means its fitting and shape, and it goes back to the weft of cloth. Istalḥama al-ṭarīq means he followed the road or followed its broadest part, as if he made himself like the weft of the warp. Istalḥama al-ṭarīq also means it widened, as if he sought what would fill it, i.e., close it. A rope that is mulāḥam, with fatḥah on the ḥāʾ, is strongly twisted, because it closed its gap as the weft closes the gap of cloth. The prophet of the malḥamah (battle) is so called because he struck the flesh with the sword; and also (of composition) as the weft gives rise to, because the purpose of his fighting (ﷺ) was the greatest good and unity. Iltaḥama al-jurḥ means the wound healed: it closed, from this, and also from flesh, because by it the wound closed. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 14:

When Allah, the Exalted, explained, as confirmation of His saying ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by, yet they turn away from it﴾ (Yusuf: 105), what He has of signs [ al-tabi'ah - ] to the attributes of perfection, among which is His being exempt from what is unfitting for His majesty and that His might is severe, He began to explain their misguidance in their association, which was pointed to in His saying: ﴿And most of them do not believe in Allah without associating [others with Him]﴾ (Yusuf: 106). [ bima - ] is the cause for concluding what precedes it, that He has no equal. (p-301) So He said: ﴿To Him is the call of truth﴾, that is, Allah, glorified is He. If anyone calls upon Him, He hears him and responds to him, if He wills, with what He wills. And if He Himself calls anyone to a matter of command, He makes clear the right course in a way that removes doubt, or a call to a ruling, and he answers humbly and complies. ﴿And those who call upon﴾, that is, the disbelievers call upon, and He shows the lowliness of their rank by His saying: ﴿besides Him﴾, that is, besides Allah, ﴿they do not respond﴾, that is, they do not bring about a response ”to them“, that is, to the disbelievers, ﴿with anything﴾. And istijabah (response) is following the caller in what he calls to, by agreeing with his will. ﴿Except as one who stretches out his hands﴾, that is, except with a response like the response of water to one who stretches out ﴿his two palms﴾. Kaffayn is the dual of kaff (palm), which is the place where the hand grasps, and its root is from kaffahu, when he gathers its edges. ﴿Toward water, that it may reach﴾, that is, that the water may reach ”his mouth“ without his palms reaching the water. This is indicated by the transitivity (ta'diyah) with ”ila“ (toward). So water does not answer his call by reaching into it. ﴿And it is not one who will reach it﴾, that is, the water is not one who reaches it, that is, reaches into it. Thus for the disbelievers, ”with that,“ is the call of falsehood, just as water is an inanimate thing that does not perceive the call of this person, so it does not answer him. Their idols are likewise.

And since their calling was confined to falsehood, He said in another place ”and what is their calling“ with an explicit noun, for generality and for attaching the judgment to the attribute: ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾ (p-302), that is, those who conceal what the lights of their intellects indicate, by their objects of worship or others. ﴿Only in error﴾, because it finds no benefit for them. As for their objects of worship, they neither harm nor benefit. As for Allah, He does not respond to them because they have wasted the foundation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 15:

Since the call to the command was clear in its paths and evident in its methods throughout all of His Books, and all of them are addressed to the two observers, and He made clear the call to the judgment by His saying: ﴿To God﴾, that is, the Supreme King, ﴿prostrates﴾, that is, submits, yields, and humbles himself, as He made clear at His saying ﴿and they will not cease to differ﴾ [Hud: 118], ﴿except those upon whom your Lord has mercy﴾ [Hud: 119], ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, to all His executed judgments and flowing decrees, ''willingly'' (ṭaw'an). Ṭaw' is yielding to a command to which one is called by one's own self. ﴿And unwillingly﴾ (karhan). Al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, said: The disbeliever is in the status of one who prostrates, even if he does not do so, because of the pressing need that he has for submission. Know that the prostration of every category is its humbling, its subjugation, and its yielding to what is intended for it. So every existing thing, whether inanimate, rational animal, non-rational, spiritual, or non-spiritual, is subjected to the command of the One to whom belongs creation and command. Shaykh Muhyi al-Din al-Nawawi, may God be pleased with him, said in his commentary on al-Muhadhdhab: Its origin, that is, prostration, is submission and humbling. Whoever humbles himself and submits has prostrated. The prostration of every created thing in the Qur'an is its obedience to what it has been subjected to. This is its origin in the language. Then the term was applied to one who places his forehead on the ground: he prostrated, because it is the utmost degree of submission.

(p-303) Since shadows are subjected to what He, glory be to Him, wills, and no one has any power to change this in any way, He said: ﴿And their shadows﴾, that is, likewise prostrate [to Him] by their extension upon the earth, shortening at times with the rising of the sun and lengthening at other times with its descent. They cannot prevent their shadows from this wherever they have shadows. ﴿In the mornings﴾ is the plural of ghadāh, which is the early part of the day, the beginning of daytime, ﴿and the evenings﴾ is the plural of aṣīl, always in all lands, and in the middle of the day in some lands. The ẓill (shadow) is the cover of a person over what is opposite to him. The fay' is that which returns after its light has gone. The aṣīl is the evening, what lies between the afternoon prayer and sunset. It is as if it makes the night, from which it arises, a root (aṣṣala al-layl alladhī yanshaʾu minhu).

The root ṣ-l-w (ṣalā), which has weak-letter, hamzated and unhamzated forms, with its eleven permutations, namely: ṣalawa, ṣawala, [laṣawa], lawaṣa, waṣala, ṣaliya, ṣayala, laṣaya, layaṣa, aṣala, ṣa'ala, revolves around connection (al-waṣālah). So ṣalāh is a link between the servant and his Lord, whether it is supplication, seeking forgiveness, mercy, or good praise from God (p-304) upon His Messenger, or the ritual with its pillars. The ṣalawāt of the Jews for their places of worship are from this in origin. Al-ṣalā is the middle of the back of us, or of every quadruped, or what slopes down from the two hips, [or] the gap between the buttock and the tail. It may be [from this, because it draws close to the other limbs when the animal bends], or it may be likened to the crooked stick by which one makes the fire, the musallī (one who warms). The she-camel's ṣalwayān (hip-area) became loose (aṣallat al-nāqah wa-ṣaliyat) when her birth was near. The musalli among horses of a race is the one that comes right after the leader, for it follows him closely. The donkey ṣallā his she-ass: he drove her and forced her onto the road, so it is as if he straightened her after she was crooked, or he meant to couple with her. A man ṣāla ṣawlah when he attacked and exalted himself, because that is continuous connection by way of compulsion and domination. [And] likewise the stallion ṣāla over the camels when he fought them, and the wild ass when he attacked a herd of wild cattle and broke it. ṣāla ʿalā kadhā: he leapt. ṣāwalahu: he leapt at him. The taṣwīl is your bringing out a thing with water, because that is the cause of purity, and when a thing is pure its parts are connected, because that exit was a barrier between them. Also, the taṣwīl is sweeping the sides of the threshing floor, because it is a cause of the connection of what was scattered. From this is al-maṣūl, like minbar: a thing in which colocynth is soaked so that its bitterness goes away. And bahāʾ: the broom. And al-ṣīlah, with kasra: the knot of the tassel, so that the place of the knot connects part with part, and by it the joining of part of the turban to part is held firm. And the locust ṣāla in its place of pasture, from taṣwīl, that is, it is churned, meaning it is mixed by turning over, so that what was scattered from it becomes connected. Ṣāla yaṣīlu is a dialect form of yaṣūlu. ṣīla lahu, with kasra: it was made easy and made available to him, because it became accompanying to him. laṣṣawtu al-rajul: I disparaged him and slandered him, because you connected disgrace to him. Fulān lā yalṣū ilā rībah: he does not join with a suspicion, that is, he is not joined to it nor added to it. al-lawṣ: a glimpse through a gap in a door and the like, like mulāwaṣah. It is as if it were a connection by looking from a place not usually visited, or because it is the cause of the connection to what is wanted. Lāwaṣa: he looked, as if he were in a state of unbalance in order to attempt a matter. And the tree: he wanted to cut it with an axe, (p-306) so he lāwaṣa in his looking right and left, how he would come to it and how he would strike it, because the result of that is connection in a manner of intensity, as was mentioned earlier in ṣāla ʿalayhi. Talawwaṣa: he twisted and turned, and from it ulīṣa, that is, he trembled. Alāṣahu ʿalā al-shayʾ: he turned it upon it and wanted it from him, as if he sought from him continuous connection. al-lawwāṣ, like saḥāb: falūdh (a sweet dish), like mulawwaṣ like muʿaẓẓam, and pure honey, because it is fit for connection. Lawaṣa: he ate. al-lawṣ: pain of the ear and the throat; al-lawṣah: pain of the back, as if because of its intensity no other connector to the body exists. Lāṣa: he deviated, that is, he removed connection. And the waṣlah, which is the axis of the root, and as if it were the reality from which its branches divided, is joining, and it is the fitting together of one thing with another. Whatever is connected to a thing, what is between them is a waṣlah, and its opposite is separation. al-waṣl is the opposite of cutting. al-awṣāl are the joints and the gathering place of bones, because they are the place of connection of one bone with another. al-waṣlān, with kasra and damma: the two layers of the back, and it is said they are the coccyx and the thigh. al-waṣīlah: a ewe that gives birth to a male and then gives birth to a female, so she connects with her brother. About it there is much disagreement, all of which revolves around connection. waṣala al-shayʾ bi-al-shayʾ: (p-307) to his mother. waṣala al-shayʾ wa-ilā al-shayʾ: he delivered it and reached it. awṣalahu, and ittaṣala: it was not cut off. waṣalahu and wāṣalahu: both occur in the chastity of love and in its licentiousness. al-waṣāʾil, plural of waṣīlah, for striped red Yemeni garments which people take as coats of mail, slit on both sides, as if because they are connected to others, or some of them are cut and then connected with them to become coats of mail. al-waṣīlah: prosperity, fertility, companionship, and the sword, because that is fit to be connected. al-waṣīlah: a ball of thread, because of the intense entanglement of some of it with others. The wide earth, because its connection was not blocked by mountains between it. laylat al-waṣl: the last nights of the month, because it connects the two months. ḥarf al-waṣl: the letter that comes after the rawiyy, because it connects the vowel of the rawiyy. waṣīlaka: whoever enters and exits with you. Taṣil: a well in the lands of Hudhayl. ittaṣala al-rajul: when he claimed lineage, because he connected himself with those to whom he claimed lineage. al-mawṣūl: an insect like the dabur that stings people, as if it were from deprivation. ṣalaytu al-laḥm: I roasted the meat, because you connected it with the fire. ṣallaytahu: you threw it into the fire for burning. al-ṣilāʾ, like kisāʾ: (p-308) roasting or the fire, like al-ṣalā in both. And it is as if from this: ṣalā ʿaṣāhu ʿalā al-nār, that is, he heated it so as to straighten it, because each of them connected it to the fire for correction. aṣlaytuhu al-nār: I made him enter it and dwell in it. ṣalā yadahu bi-al-nār: he warmed it, because he connected it to it. ṣaliya al-nār, like raḍiya: he endured its heat. ṣalaytu fulānan: I tried him, deceived him, and cheated him; all of that is for the purpose of connecting with him for a matter. al-ṣilāyah, with hamza optional: the forehead, because of its frequent contact with the ground in prayer, and the mortar for perfume, because of the continuous pounding. ṣalaytu li-al-ṣayd taṣliyah: when you set a trap for it so that it falls into it and you reach it. From this is the hadith: "Indeed for Satan there are maṣāliyy and fukhūkh," the plural of miṣlāh and fakh. al-ṣilyān, with kasra then shadda: Al-Qazzaz said in Mukhtaṣar al-ʿAyn: a known plant. Al-Qazzaz said: it is a tree that has a large root, which sometimes is stripped of its center while what is around it grows, and it is among the best pastures, and it is the bread of the camels. It is said that horses eat it, and its color is reddish-white. End quote.

It was named thus because camels frequently connect with it. And ṣīt al-rajul, like rimīt and riḍīt: when I disparaged him and slandered him with immorality. Al-Qazzaz said: it is said that it is to attribute him to a suspicious party. laṣiya ilayhi: he joined him for a suspicion. Lāṣa yalīṣu: he deviated. Luṣtuhu ulīṣuhu and alaṣtuhu: when I disturbed him or moved him so that he would pull himself away, as if it were from deprivation. alaṣtuhu ʿan kadhā: when I sought him away from it. It is possible that it is deprivation and it is possible that it is affirmation. And al-aṣl: the bottom of every thing, because all things are connected to it. aṣṣala, like karuma: became possessed of a root, or became firm or established, like taʾaṣṣala. And al-raʾy: it was sound. All of this is a likeness to the root. al-aṣīl: one who has a root, and the firm-minded person, and he has become aṣīl like karuma. al-aṣīl: the evening, because it is the connection between day and night, or because when it announced the ending of the day, it was as if it had uprooted it from its root. From it is al-aṣīl: for destruction and death, like al-aṣīlah in both. laqītuhum muʾaṣṣilan, that is, in the evening. He took him with his whole root (bi-aṣalatihi), that is, with his entirety and his root. Aṣīlatuka: all of your property or your palm tree. al-aṣl, like katif: (p-310) the one who uproots. And aṣala ʿilman: he killed it, as if he continued its connection until he perfected it. al-aṣalah, with fatha on the first and second: a short snake that attacks a person, said in Mukhtaṣar al-ʿAyn. In al-Qamus: a small or large snake that kills by its breath. If one considers the attacking, it is from connection, as was mentioned earlier in ṣāla ʿalayhi. If one considers the destruction, it is from uprooting. Aṣl al-māʾ, like faraḥa: it became foul from mud. And the meat: it changed. It may be from the connection, that is, because of the intense connection of mud to water and of air to meat. It may be from aṣīl, that is, destruction in its entirety and its root. It may be from the deprivation of connection. Ṣaʾula al-baʿīr, like karuma ṣaʾālah: it leapt at people, or [became] one that kills people and attacks them. Ṣahīl al-faras: its neighing, because of the connection of its tones. This has passed at His saying, exalted is He, in [Surat Hud], peace be upon him: ﴿Does your prayer command you﴾ [Hud: 87], as an indication of this. And God, glory be to Him and exalted, knows best.

[p-311] So when it became certain that He, glory be to Him, is the one who manages the heavens and the earth and who prevails over whatever is in them, and it became certain that lordship over both belongs to Him alone, He commanded that the question be directed at them about this, as a refutation of the idol-worshippers and others among the heretics. He said: ﴿Say﴾, that is, after you have set forth these decisive proofs, establishing for them ﴿Who is the Lord﴾, that is, the Creator and Manager, ﴿of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, and everything in them.
