Since it had already passed, in other verses, that they acknowledge His lordship and confess that He creates and provides, yet this did not restrain them from associating others with Him, they are here treated as though they deny it out of obstinacy. So He did not wait for their answer but commanded that the Prophet answer them with what they would themselves answer, indicating that they do not shy away from contradiction in following their desires, and that their supposedly noble intellects and their inherited opinions, in their own claim, do not protect them from falling into the pits of destruction. So He said: ﴿Say: Allah﴾, that is, the One to whom the whole affair belongs. Thereby it is established that there is no protector except Him. Consequently, rebuke is directed at them for relying on other than Him, and He commanded the Prophet to rebuke them in His saying: ﴿Say: Have you then taken﴾, that is, have you, on account of His sole lordship over you, taken to the utmost of desire, so that you have made association the cause of what should be the cause of monotheism, ﴿other than Him as protectors﴾, which do not equal you in causing harm or benefit. Rather, ﴿they have no power over their own selves﴾, so how could they have power over others, ﴿for benefit﴾ [or harm]. It is indefinite so as to be general, and it is placed first because the context concerns their seeking from them, and a person seeks only what benefits him.

Since it is known that no one has the power to produce an effect in another that he cannot produce in himself, He said: ﴿nor harm﴾. Thus it is established that whoever equates them with Allah is the most misguided of the misguided, because he must equate opposites. So the meaning of His saying: ﴿Say: Is the blind equal﴾ to the seeing? Equality (istiwa') means the continuance of a thing in one direction. ﴿The blind﴾ in his eye or in his heart, ﴿and the seeing﴾ likewise, ﴿or are the darknesses and the light equal﴾ in any respect? Have their intellects led them to equate these utterly opposite things, which are so clearly distinct, out of stupidity or obstinacy, to the point of equating the One who creates with the one who does not create? Thus they assigned to Him a partner, likewise out of stupidity or obstinacy. ﴿Or have they assigned to Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses all the attributes of greatness, [p-313] ﴿partners﴾.

Then He explained what might constitute the partnership, saying, describing them: ﴿who created as He creates﴾, and as a consequence of this He said: ﴿so that creation seemed similar to them﴾. Similarity (tashabbuh) is the resemblance of things in such a way that they become confused, so that one cannot distinguish between the two things. ﴿The creation seemed alike to them﴾. So that creation which the partners made became the cause of a doubt arising for them. He put this in the third person to indicate that they are fit to be turned away from, since they belong among the cattle, for they say what does not reason in any way. This is close to what comes shortly after in His saying: ﴿or with an apparent word﴾ [13:33], that is, with a doubt having some appearance of plausibility to certain minds.

Since it is known with certainty that their answer would be that all creation belongs to Allah, and that this did not prevent them from worshipping others, He commanded him to answer them while turning away from their answer, and He said: ﴿Say: Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King, ﴿is the Creator of all things﴾, indicating that in their conduct they are like one who denies this out of obstinacy, or who tears the veil of modesty and rends the garment of decency. Since it has been established that He alone is the Creator, it is necessary that He alone be worshipped in divinity, so He said: ﴿And He is the One﴾, who has no like among things, whereas everything [p-314] other than Him has a kind that resembles it. How can the rank of one who has a like be compared with the rank of One who has no like? ﴿The Irresistible﴾, before whose domination everything is subdued by its own self and shadows, and who is capable in a way that no conqueror can overcome Him, while He overcomes everything. This is an indication, as has passed in similar contexts more than once, in Surah [Yusuf] and elsewhere, to the proof of mutual exclusion (burhan al-tamanu'), for their lords are many. If they had life and were disposing of the dominion, mutual contention would have been possible among them, and each of them would have been exposed to being subdued. How much more so when they are inanimate! Thus it is established with certainty that none of them is fit for divinity under any supposition. Al-Rummani said: "The one (wahid) is of two kinds: a thing that is not divisible at all, and a thing that is not divisible in meaning, like the world."

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 17:**

Since the carrying of water on high is only possible by force, and its sending down at one time rather than another is likewise [by Allah's decree], He followed this sealing with His words, as a visible proof of it: ﴿He sends down﴾. Since sending down is sometimes used figuratively for bringing into existence something whose bringing into existence is great, He confirmed its matter with His words: ﴿from the sky﴾. Since what is sent down from it is of various kinds, He said: ﴿water, so the valleys flow﴾, meaning that because of its abundance the sending down caused [p. 315] the valleys to flow ﴿with their measure﴾. ﴿Valleys﴾ means their waters, both large and small. The *wadi* (valley) is the base of a great mountain opposite which lies another mountain or a hill, so that rain gathers in it and flows through its expanse. From the same root comes *diyah* (blood-money), the large sum of wealth paid in place of a killing. ﴿With its measure﴾: *qadr* is the proportion of a thing to another without excess or deficiency. The meaning is that the waters filled the valleys in due proportion, together with what this indicates of the singling out of Lordship, and this is an example of truth and falsehood, which is His saying: ﴿So the torrent carries﴾. *Ihtimal* (carrying) is lifting a thing upon the back by the strength of the one who carries it. ﴿The torrent﴾ is rain-water flowing from the valley with force, ﴿foam swelling up﴾, meaning high, rising by its swelling. *Zabad* (foam) is the froth that rises on water, and the root's core is lightness, which entails height. From it come *zabad al-bahr* (sea-foam) and *zabad al-ba'ir* (the froth coming out of a camel's mouth) and the angry person's foam. *Zabadat al-mar'atu al-qutn* means the woman fluffed the cotton when she carded it. *Zabad* (with the pattern *kurrumān*) is a kind of plant whose branches spread out. *Shah muzbidah* means a fat sheep. From it also comes *zabad* (civet), the known perfume, which is a filth resembling froth that gathers under the tail of a kind of civet cat. From it also comes *zubd* (with a *damma* and a sukun) for pure milk, since it is the lightest part. It is said: *zabadtu fulanan uzabduhu*, meaning I fed so-and-so butter, and then the usage was extended until it was said of any gift in general. From this is the hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the gift of the polytheists." From it also comes *zidb* (with a *kasra* then a sukun), which means share. It is possible that the *zabad* of plants comes from the *zubd* of milk, since it is good pasture; as if it was likened to it, or because it is its cause. Likewise *shah muzbadah* means a fat sheep, and lightness entails quickness. It is said *tuzbidu al-yamin*, meaning he hastened to it, or it was likened to butter in the ease with which it is swallowed.

Since foam is the best parable for their worshipped things, and since it is not restricted to water, which is by nature liquid, gathering filth and refuse through its flow, He mentioned along with it what resembles it in benefit, namely solid hard substances that foam when melted, while in their solid state they are of utmost purity and freedom from impurities, as is apparent. So He said: ﴿And from what they kindle﴾, meaning kindling that rises ﴿upon it﴾, meaning for melting, ﴿in the fire﴾, from metals, ﴿seeking an ornament﴾ with which you adorn yourselves, such as bracelets, rings and the like, ﴿or﴾ seeking ﴿a commodity﴾ which you enjoy, such as dirhams, dinars, swords [p. 317] and vessels [and the like]. The root of *mata'* (commodity) is present enjoyment. This is an exhaustive division of the kinds of metal mentioned, along with showing disdain for it, even though people compete for it [as is the custom of kings, who show glory and pride by scorning what people compete for]. ﴿Foam like it﴾, meaning like the foam of water, which is skimmed from its surface or clings to the edges of the vessel so that it departs, and that substance remains pure, like truth when doubts have departed from it and suspicions have been dispelled.

Since this is most beautiful and most fitting to the intended meaning, the hearer is bound to be moved and say: "Only Allah the Exalted can produce a parable like this! How wonderful a parable!" So His words are answered: ﴿Thus﴾, meaning like this kind, lofty in rank, strange in wonder, firm in cause, ﴿Allah strikes﴾, i.e. He to whom all command belongs, ﴿the truth and falsehood﴾, [i.e.] their likeness. *Darb al-mathal* (striking a parable) is making it travel through the lands so that people may take it as a model.

Since by this distinction He alerted to the exalted rank of this parable, He began to explain it, saying first with what is most important in this context, which is the refutation of the falsehood that misled them, [p. 318] and He divided it according to the scattered, jumbled order: ﴿As for the foam﴾, meaning what [is] a parable for absolute falsehood, ﴿it passes away﴾, clinging to trees and the sides of valleys, because it floats by its lightness and clings to dense things by its density. ﴿As scum﴾. Abu Hayyan said: meaning dissolved and scattered, without benefit in it and without permanence. Ibn al-Anbari said: scattered, from *jafa'at al-rih al-ghayma*, when the wind cut the cloud apart, and *jafa'at al-rajul*, when it threw him down. End of quotation. This is the parable of falsehood, consisting of doubts and suspicions and what the people of obstinacy stir up. It has no permanence, even if it circulates for a while, a trial by which Allah tests His servants so that the firm may be distinguished from the shaken. Then it quickly perishes. Al-Rummani said: *al-juffa'* is the place of a thing being emptied out until it perishes. ﴿But as for what benefits people﴾, of water and metal, which is like the truth, ﴿it remains in the earth﴾. People benefit from the water by which every thing lives, and from the metal by which things are completed. Water and ore are like the Qur'an, because in it are the life of hearts and the continuance of the Law, just as water revives dead lands, and ores revive the deadness of livelihood and organize transactions which require people to mix with one another and be bound together by need. Valleys and vessels are like hearts: there remains in them what they can bear, according to the breadth and narrowness of the heart, in accordance with purity and the strength of understanding.

When this parable had been concluded with this explanation, which the two species of jinn and humankind would fail to match, because it is the most excellent in meaning with the most concise expression and the clearest indication, it was as if it was said: "Does everything become clear with this clarity?" So it was said: "Yes":
﴿Thus﴾, meaning like that kind, ﴿Allah strikes﴾, i.e. He to whom belongs complete encompassment in knowledge and power, ﴿the parables﴾, making them most clear, even though they are most obscure.

The root *j-f-a* has forms with waw, with ya, hamzated and unhamzated, in every order: *ja'a, ja'fa, faja'a*; *jafiya, jiyafa, fayaja*; *jafawa, jawafa, fawaja*; *fajawa* and *jafa*. All of them revolve around throwing away. *Jafa'a al-wadi wa al-qadar* means he cast out, by throwing away the foam, and *jafa'a al-qadar wa al-wadi* means he wiped off its scum, i.e. threw it out. *Jaf'ahu* means he threw him down. *Al-barmah fi al-qas'ah* means it covered it, i.e. the casting out of what is in it. *Al-bab* means he closed it and opened it, which are opposites, because in both cases it is like something thrown. *Al-baql* means uprooting it from its base. *Al-jafa'* (with the pattern *ʿuzzab*) means falsehood, because it is fit to be cast off and thrown away. A *safinah khaliyah* (empty ship) is so called because we are about to have water cast against it.

*Ajfa mashiyatahu* means he exhausted his livestock by travel and did not feed them, i.e. he drove them as if he were casting them away. *Jafa'a bihi* means he threw it. *Jafat al-bilad* means its good went away, so it was cast out, or it became fit to be cast out and removed. *Al-'am jafat ibiluna* means that most of them gave birth prematurely, because they cast out their foetuses.

From the ya-form: *jafaytuhu ujfihi* means I threw him down. *Al-jufayah* (with a *damma*) is an empty ship, and *al-mujfi* is one who is cast off.

From the waw-form: *jafa al-shay'u yajfu* means it did not remain in its place, as if it was separated from its place and thrown off. *Al-jafa'* and *al-jafwah* mean abandoning kinship. *Ijtafaytuhu* means I removed it from its place. *Jafa 'alayhi kadha* means it became heavy, so it became fit to be thrown off and separated from him. A *rajul jafi al-khilqah wa al-khuluq* is harsh and coarse, because when a thing becomes coarse it does not stick like a delicate thing. *Ajfa al-mashiyah* means he followed them and did not let them eat. [p. 321] *Fihi jafwah* means he is harsh; if he is treated harshly, it is said *bihi jafwah*.

From its hamzated reversal: *jaffa-hu*, meaning he threw him down and terrified him, i.e. cast fear into his heart. *Al-shajarah* means he uprooted it from its base. *Al-ja'af* (with the pattern *shaddad*) means shouting, as if he casts with his voice. A *rajul mujaff* is one without steadiness, as if he is cast from his place. *Al-majwuf* is one who is hungry or terrified, as if from *al-jawf* (the belly), though its first waw was made hamzah because of its *damma*, although it is possible to interpret it as meaning that this was cast into him.

From the ya-form: *al-jifah* is the corpse of a dead person, and it has rotted. *Al-jiyaf* (with the pattern *shiddad*) is a grave-robber. *Jafat tajif* means it stank, so it became ready to be thrown and buried. *Jayyafahu* means he struck him, because he saw him fit for distance. *Jayyafa fulan fi kadha wa jauffa* means he was frightened and frightened others, i.e. fear was cast into his heart, so that no land could contain him, but he cast himself from place to place.

From the waw-form: *al-jawf* is the low ground [of the earth], because it contains what is cast into it and holds it, and whatever is thrown from the mountains settles in it. *Al-jawf minka* is your belly, because it needs food to be cast into it. The people of the lowlands call the tents of their workers *al-ajwaf*, because they cast themselves and their goods into them. *Jawf al-layl* is its middle, a figure of speech likened to the belly. *Al-ajwafan* are the belly and the private parts. *Al-jawf* (with the pattern *muharrakah*) means breadth. *Al-jawfa'* of buckets is the wide one, and of spears and trees is the empty one. *Al-ja'ifah* is a wound that reaches the belly. *Walt'uhu ja'ifah* means a deep pit, because by its depth it resembles a hollow more than a mountain. *Jawa'if al-nafs* are the hollows of the belly in the seats of the spirit. *Al-mujawwaf* (with the pattern *mu'azzam*) is one without a heart, as if his heart was cast out of his belly and became empty. *Al-juwfan* (with a *damma*) is a donkey's penis, because of the breadth of its belly. *Ajaftu al-bab* means I shut it. It is as if it is from deprivation, because you blocked the belly of the house, or because it likened the locking to casting out the door.

From the hamzated reversal: *fajiahu al-amr* (with the patterns of *sami'a* and *mana'a*) means he came upon him without his noticing, as if it was thrown at him. *Futji'at al-naqah* (with the pattern of *fariha*) means her belly grew large, as if something was thrown into it. [p. 323] *Fajaa* (with the pattern of *mana'a*) means he had intercourse with her, because he cast her down and cast himself upon her. *Al-mufaji'* is the lion, because it comes out suddenly and leaps without pausing.

From the waw-reversal: *al-fajwah* is the wide space of land and the gap, because it is prepared for what is cast into it. *Al-fajwah* also means the courtyard of a house and what lies between the edges of the hooves, i.e. their right and left sides. *Fajja qawsahu* means he raised it and drew its string away from its belly, so it is *fajwa'*. *Fajja babahu* means he opened it, so it became like a hollow. *Al-fajā* is the distance between the two knees, or the two thighs, or the two shins, or the two hamstrings of a camel. *Fajiya* (with the pattern of *radiya*) means he is *afja*. It means also the largeness of a she-camel's belly; the verb is like the verb. *Al-tafjiyah* is uncovering, because you cast off the covering. *Al-tafjiyah* also means removal, which is clear in casting. *Afja* means he widened the expense on his dependants, as if he was throwing it out with a cast.

From the ya-reversal: *afaja al-rajul* means he hastened. From it comes *al-fayj*, the messenger of the ruler, on foot, as if because of his speed he is cast down upon the earth. This [p. 324] is the correct view, which the author of *al-'Ubab* established, because it is an Arabization of *bek*. It was also said that it is waw-form, originally *fayawaj*, then *fayaj* (like *kayis*), then lightened. Its plural is *al-fuyuj*. It was also said that *al-fuyuj* are those who enter the prison, leave it and guard it. *Afaja fi al-ardi* means he went away. *Al-qawm* means they went away and dispersed, as if he cast them out. *Al-fayj* is a low, level depression of the earth, because it is a place where what is above is cast.

From the waw-reversal: *al-fawj* means a group, as if they were cut off from the multitude and cast out. *Faja al-misk* means it spread and emitted fragrance, i.e. its scent spread out. *Al-nahar* means cold; either in the sense that it casts its cold upon what is in it, or because it makes living creatures need something to cast upon them to warm them. *Afaja* means he hastened, ran, and sent the camels to the watering-place in groups. *Al-fatij* is a wide expanse of land, because it prepares it for what is cast into it, by naming the place after its state. *Afaja fi 'adwihi* means he was slow. This is for negation. *Fajat al-naqah bi rajilaha* means the she-camel kicked with her two hind legs behind her. *Al-fa'ijah* is the wide space between every two heights, as if it is the place where what descends from them is cast.

From its reversal: *wajafa yajifu wajifan* means he was agitated. *Al-wajf* is a kind of pace of camels and horses. *Wajafa yajifu*, *awjafatuhu*, and *istawjafa al-hubbu fu'adahu* means love took his heart away, as if he had cast it out of him.

---

(p-325) Since the states of truth and falsehood in themselves, in their stability and instability, had been completed, he mentioned what belongs to their people of reward and punishment, as an answer to one who seems to say: "What of the one who reflects upon these parables and turns away from the misguidance they point to, or deviates from what they call to and inclines away from it?" So it was answered with His words: ﴿For those who responded﴾, meaning those who sought from themselves the response and brought it into being, ﴿to their Lord﴾, meaning the One who does good to them, out of gratitude to Him, ﴿is the best [reward]﴾, meaning the one magnificent in goodness, which is abiding in the Garden. That is their recompense. Abu Hayyan said: "That is victory in this world, and what they were singled out with of His blessings, may He be exalted, and entry into the Garden in the Hereafter." End of quotation. It has already been mentioned in [Surah Yunus] that peace be upon him, that they will be increased in what no one knows the measure of, except the One for whom they did that out of fear of His punishment and hope for His reward.

When he had mentioned what is for the obedient, he followed it with the recompense of the disobedient, saying, beginning: ﴿And those who did not respond﴾, meaning those who do not desire to bring the response into being to Him. He informed about this beginning with His words, making known that their hastening for the punishment, by their hastening for evil before good, is audacity arising from pure ignorance, which disappears when they see His punishment, may He be glorified. At that time they will exert all effort in ransom, yet nothing will be accepted from them: ﴿If indeed they had whatever is in the earth﴾, (p-326) meaning under their ownership and within their power, ﴿all of it, and the like of it with it, they would surely ransom themselves with it.﴾ He emphasized this with His words ﴿all of it﴾, and clarified it with His words ﴿with it﴾, meaning they would make the redemption of their souls at the utmost of their effort. He emphasized it because of the disbelievers' claim that they are never humbled by anything and nothing weakens their strength. Ransom (al-iftida', "ransoming") is making one of two things a substitute for the other, in the manner of protection by it. So it is as if it were said: "What has befallen them, that their state is this?" It was said, indicating that the ransom will not be accepted from them even if it is great: ﴿Those are the ones for whom is the evil reckoning.﴾ The reckoning (al-hisab) is the counting of what is upon the servant and what is his, and the evil of the accountability, and the absence of pardon for anything. ﴿And their abode is Hell﴾, meaning their resting place, ﴿Hell﴾, meaning the level into which they will be cast with its frowning and sullenness. And since the abode is only where its occupant seeks rest by reclining upon bedding and the like, he said, expressing it with the gathering of blameworthy things: ﴿And wretched is the resting place.﴾

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 19:

When the states of the one who responded and the one who turned away diverged in the matter of recompense, and what preceded had been complete, the discourse turned to clarifying the matter through particulars and examples, together with encouragement and warning. It was therefore fitting that the effect be arranged upon it, and there followed from it a denunciation of (p-327) those who equated the learned person who acts with others, with a turn (iltifat, a shift in grammatical address) to His saying ﴿Are the blind and the seeing alike?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16], and who equated the truth with falsehood, with a turn to His saying ﴿Thus God strikes the truth and falsehood﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17]. So His saying ﴿Is then (afa-man)﴾, with the fa' of causation, is well chosen. ﴿He who knows﴾ means one who has beneficial knowledge and acts upon it. ﴿Only﴾, i.e., the one who ﴿has been sent down﴾, i.e., whose sending down has been found and completed, ﴿to you from your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who is good to you with the best of management, ﴿the truth﴾, i.e., perfect in truthfulness. He is the one whose eye is luminous for sight and whose heart is luminous for insight and reflection. He is guided by what he knows to the path of right guidance so that he follows it, and to the path of error so that he abandons it. He understands the signs and benefits from the far-travelling examples, just as one sees with the eye the path of salvation from the path of destruction. ﴿Is like one who is blind﴾, having neither sight nor insight, because he does not act even if he is learned, and so he does not benefit from the examples. It is as if it were said: they are not alike at all as a comparison. Then he gave the reason for this denunciation in His saying: ﴿Only﴾, i.e., because he only knows this by remembrance, and only ﴿those who remember﴾, i.e., who seek remembrance with great earnestness, so that they act, ﴿the people of﴾, i.e., possessors of, ﴿understanding (al-albab)﴾, i.e., the pure and sincere intellects, receptive to remembrance through reflection on the fact that what has been sent down from God is firm in its foundations [firm in its bases, with no one able to remove any of its meanings or demolish any part of its structures], and that whatever is other than it is a flimsy weave with weak strands, loose in its joints, its traces effaced, its signposts obliterated, its paths unknown, its regions dark, and its perils numerous. As for the heart that does not turn back from its error in response to such clarification, it is as if it were not receptive to remembrance, so it deserves to be counted as non-existent, and remembrance is specifically attributed to the heart. It is known that one who has understanding and one who has none are not alike. Understanding (lubb) and heart (qalb) are the most noble, purest, and finest part of a thing.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 20:

When Allah, glorified is He, granted them among themselves the capacity for remembrance through the intellects that point to His oneness and submission to His commands, it was as if it were a covenant in that regard. So He said, describing those who remember with what definitively indicates that there is no intellect other than theirs: ﴿Those who fulfil﴾, i.e., who bring about fulfilment for everything, ﴿the covenant of Allah﴾, i.e., [because of] the firm contract (*'ahd*) from the Supreme King regarding His commands and prohibitions. So they do each of the two as He has laid down for them, and do not put one of them in the place of the other. *'Ahd* (covenant): the contract that precedes the command about what one does or avoids. *Iifa'* (fulfilment): making a thing equal to another without excess or deficiency.

(p-٣٢٩) Since rational proof necessarily requires steadfastness in it, just as the verbal covenant (*mithaq*) requires fulfilment of it, He, exalted, said: ﴿and do not break the covenant﴾, i.e., the binding, nor the bond, nor its place, nor its time. *Naqd* (breaking): undoing the contract by doing what contradicts it and cannot be valid together with it. *Mithaq* (covenant): the firm contract, which is the commands and prohibitions affirmed by the judgment of reason.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 21:

Since the command of God proceeds along the path of reason, even though reason falls short of it and cannot attain it without a guide, He said: ﴿And those who join﴾, that is, from everything, on a continuous basis, ﴿what God has commanded﴾, that is, the One to whom all command belongs; and He said: ﴿to be joined with it﴾ rather than "to join it," so that they are commanded to join it twice, and so that it conveys the renewal of joining whenever a severer cuts it, on a continuous basis, because of what is supported on this by the two proofs of reason (ʿaql) and transmitted text (naql). And wasl (joining) is adding the second to the first without a gap.

Since the proof guides to the fact that God, exalted is He, is both hoped for and feared, He said: ﴿and they fear their Lord﴾, that is, the One who does good to them, lest He take vengeance on them if they oppose Him by cutting off the good. And since reason, after the alerting of the messengers, points to the power over the return by the power over the origin, and fear of Him is greatest [of fears], God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they dread﴾, that is, they bring about dread continuously, ﴿the evil of the reckoning﴾, which is its being scrutinized without pardon. From the beginning of the surah to here is an elaboration of His saying at the beginning of al-Baqarah: ﴿This is the Book, there is no doubt in it, a guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], with regard also to His saying at the end of Yusuf: ﴿It was not a narration that could be invented﴾ [Yusuf: 111].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 22:

Since fulfilling the covenant is extremely difficult for the self, he said, pointing to that while including others as well: ﴿Those who patiently persevere⦆ — that is, in obedience to Allah and in abstaining from His disobedience, and in everything in which patience is appropriate. Patience (al-sabr) is restraint (al-habs), and it is the swallowing of the bitterness of denying the self what it loves, of what is not lawful to do. ﴿Seeking⦆ — that is, desiring ﴿the countenance of their Lord⦆ — that is, the One who is good to them. He mentioned "the countenance" as a way of stirring up modesty and urging it, not so that it might be said, "How steadfast he is!", nor because one is blamed for impatience, nor because there is no benefit in panic or in fear of being mocked.

Since the individual instances of a thing may differ in nobility, he singled out for mention things that fall within the covenant and the pact, to honor them. So he said: ﴿and establish the prayer⦆, because it stands in the same relation to the connection with Allah as the covenant stands to the one who makes the covenant with Him. And he said: ﴿and spend⦆, and he lightened the burden on them by specifying a part, saying: ﴿out of what We have provided them⦆ — because spending is among the greatest means that lead to one's aims. This is spending of wealth; that is spending of the faculties. And he said: ﴿secretly and openly⦆, as an indication of urging the equality of the two states, alerting to sincerity. It is permissible that what is meant by "secretly" is what it is appropriate to keep private, such as voluntary acts, and by "openly" what is recommended to make public, such as obligatory acts, unless some impediment prevents it. This is an elaboration of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who establish the prayer and spend out of what We have provided them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], and ﴿Seek help in patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45].

And he said: ﴿and they repel⦆ — that is, they push back with strength and insight ﴿evil⦆ with ﴿good⦆ — that is, with speech or action. This is an indication of abandoning retaliation, or that they follow the evil with good, which then erases it, out of fear and hope, and as an urging toward all righteous deeds. So this is the outcome of works of piety and the rank of those brought near.

Since He concluded the previous verse with what points to the afterlife as a warning, He concluded this one with the like of it as an encouragement, saying: ﴿Those — that is, the people of high rank — ﴿for them is the good final abode⦆.

Al-Biqa'i's commentary on Surah 13, verse 23:

He explained it by His saying: ﴿Gardens of perpetual abode﴾, i.e., a long-lasting dwelling. From the same root comes al-ma'din (the mine, a place where things remain and settle) [and it is the highest of the gardens]. Then he began to explain their settling therein, saying: ﴿They will enter them﴾.

Since a home is not good without the beloved, he said, conjoining it to the pronoun of subject (indicating that a lineage devoid of righteousness is of no benefit): ﴿and whoever was righteous﴾. Ṣalāḥ (righteousness) is the soundness of one's condition in accordance with what reason and the Sharia call for. ﴿Among their fathers﴾, i.e., those who were the cause of their existence; ﴿and their spouses and their offspring﴾, i.e., those who came about through them. Then he increased the encouragement with His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them﴾, because the frequent coming of the messengers of the King is greater in honor and more abundant in joy and dignity.

(p-332) Since their coming from the customary places, while having the ability to use others, is more indicative of courtesy and honor, He said: ﴿from every gate﴾, saying to them:

﴿Salamun ʿalaykum﴾ (Peace be upon you). As-salam: a greeting of honour, free from every trace of harm. He then made clear that the cause of this peace is patience, saying: ﴿bi-ma sabartum﴾ (because of your patience), i.e., by your patience, the one for which you were patient, and the one upon which you were patient, indicating that patience is the pillar of the whole religion (ʿimad al-din). When that was complete, there followed from it His saying: ﴿fa-niʿma ʿuqba al-dar﴾ (How excellent is the final abode!), which is the dwelling in a settled place, prepared with the buildings one needs and the amenities from which one benefits. And ʿuqba (the outcome, ʿuqba): the end that results from a beginning, whether good or evil.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 25:

When he had mentioned what awaits those who are saved (al-nājīn), he mentioned the fate of those who perish, saying: ﴿And those who break the covenant of God﴾, that is, the King Most High, "so they act contrary to its requirement." Naqḍ (breaking) is separation that negates the composition of a structure. Since breaking is harmful even if it is in the smallest part, he introduced the preposition, saying: ﴿after its binding﴾, that is, the binding He tied upon them through the intellects He gave them and the power He deposited in them to arrange premises that produce the good aims, which indicate the soundness of everything His messengers, upon them be prayers, peace, greetings and honor, reported. Mīthāq (covenant) is the firm establishment of a contract in the most emphatic manner possible for its kind. ﴿And they sever what﴾, that is, the thing which ﴿God has commanded﴾, that is, without regarding His greatness and majesty. He turned away from saying "that it be joined" to what he had mentioned shortly before, and said: ﴿that it be joined﴾, that is, because of its manifest and hidden goods, which are the very essence of righteousness. ﴿And they cause corruption﴾, that is, they bring about corruption ﴿in the earth﴾, that is, in whatever part of it they are, by severing what God has commanded to be joined, following their desires, turning away from the proofs of their intellects, and making light of the vengeance of the Great, the Exalted. Since they were like this, they deserved the opposite of what was prescribed for the righteous (al-muttaqūn), and that is expulsion, punishment, wrath, retribution and the evil of the encounter. So He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿Those﴾, that is, the remote and hated ones, ﴿for them is the curse﴾, that is, expulsion and distance, ﴿and for them is the evil abode﴾, that is, their final abode will be evil, through the arrival in it of what distresses them and not what gladdens them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 26:

When the great exhortation to spending (infaq) had preceded, and it was indicated that it is among the most reliable means of connection (wasla) to all the commands of Allah, and it concluded that for the disbeliever there is distance (bu'd) and expulsion (tard) from every good and there is evil, it was the place for the disbelievers to say: "What is with us that He widens (provision) for us despite our distance, and constricts it for the believer despite his connection and attachment? And what is with him that He does not extend his provision so that he may be able to carry out what He commanded him, if that is indeed true?" So it was said: ﴿Allah﴾, i.e., the One to whom all perfection belongs, ﴿extends provision﴾, and He indicated the completeness of (p-334) His power, glory be to Him and exalted, by His saying, may His power be glorified: ﴿for whomever He wills﴾, so that he obeys in his provision or disobeys, ﴿and restricts﴾ for whomever He wills, so that He makes his provision according to the measure of his need, so that he is patient or impatient, for a wisdom whose subtleties escape thoughts. Then He makes what is with the disbeliever a cause of his abandonment, and the poverty of the believer a cause of the elevation of his station. Thus wealth is not something by which one is praised, nor is poverty something for which one is blamed [by it]; rather, one is praised and blamed by one's deeds (al-athar).

Since abundance is usually the occasion of joy, except for those whom Allah has purified, and they are fewer than the few, He said, censuring those who are reassured by it: ﴿And they rejoiced﴾, i.e., when He extended provision to them, they became insolent (bataru), disbelieved, and rejoiced ﴿in the life of this world﴾, i.e., in its completeness; [and joy (al-farah) is a pleasure in the heart at attaining what is desired. Since the world is insignificant in comparison with the abode with which He concluded for the righteous, He said, as an increase in encouragement and warning]: ﴿And the life of this world, in the Hereafter, is nothing but a fleeting enjoyment (mata')﴾, i.e., in comparison with it, [it is] petty and perishing. Al-Rummani said: "Mata' is that by which benefit is gained in the immediate present, and its root is tamatto', which is enjoying the present matter."

(p-335) When reason (*al-'aql*, the faculty of intellect) was the greatest of the proofs, and it had already been stated that it is restricted to those who take heed, this indicated that whoever is other than them is like grazing cattle. It was also known that what the Law (*al-shar'*, revelation and divine law) calls to is righteousness, and its opposite is corruption. Reason exists only to recognize righteousness so that it may be followed, and corruption so that it may be avoided. The one who seeks the sending down of a sign other than this, especially after many successive signs and manifest proofs, is a fitting object of wonder. So He said, in the manner of expressing wonder, coordinated with His saying ﴿and they rejoice﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26], and manifesting (the noun) what would normally be expressed by a pronoun, to draw attention to the attribute that caused them to be obstinate: ﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾, that is, they concealed what their reason called them to of good and of Allah's signs, out of stubbornness. ﴿Why not?﴾, that is, "Why would it not be so? What is the reason?"

Since what is known to be from the King does not need to ask about the one who brings it, His saying ﴿is sent down upon him﴾ is in the passive form. That is, this Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿A sign﴾, that is, a clear indication, ﴿from his Lord﴾, that is, the One who does good to him by answering what he asks, so that we may be guided by it and believe in him. He commanded him to answer this with His saying ﴿Say﴾, that is, to these obstinate ones: How intense is your obstinacy, since you have made this statement which includes your denial that a sign should be sent down to me, even though no one has been given signs like those given to me. Thus it is certain that sending down signs is not the cause of faith; rather, its affair is with Allah. ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, that is, the One for whom no one has any command alongside Him, ﴿leads astray whom He wills﴾, His leading astray being of those who do not turn back in repentance, but who turn away from the proof of reason and break the firm covenant of the premises that produce certainty of the truth of what the Messengers called to, because of the coarseness that has been formed in his heart. So he becomes such that he will not believe even if every sign were sent down to him, because all of them are equal in their call to what reason calls to, for whoever has reason. Indeed, before this, many signs had been sent down, which are greater proofs of the intended meaning. ﴿And He guides﴾ at the call of those who call, ﴿to Him﴾, that is, to His obedience, by the mere proof of reason without requesting a sign, ﴿whoever turns back﴾, that is, whoever has a heart inclined toward the proofs and returns to them often, because He wills his turning back, like Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and others among those who followed him, from among the ten who were given the good tidings of Paradise, and others.

Then He substituted for them ﴿those who believe﴾, meaning they brought this attribute into being, ﴿and whose hearts find rest﴾, meaning they become calm and at ease with the proof after being agitated by doubts, since they achieved tranquility after the attribute of faith, achieving it in a continuous manner that indicates the steadfastness of their faith due to their abandoning obstinacy. This present-tense verb (al-mudari') in this construction is not intended to refer to the present or the future; rather, it is intended to denote continuity of the meaning regardless of time. ﴿in the remembrance of God﴾, who is the greatest of the signs in showing that the one who is remembered possesses all the attributes of perfection. Thus the verse is of ihtibak (a rhetorical device of mutual omission): mentioning the "will" first indicates its omission second, and mentioning "turning in repentance" second indicates the omission of its opposite first.

Since this is a place where the obstinate one might say, "And who finds rest in that?", [He says]: ﴿Surely in the remembrance of God﴾, meaning Him to whom belong majesty and honour, (p-337) not in the remembrance of anything else, ﴿hearts find rest﴾, so that they become still from seeking anything other than Him. Remembrance (dhikr) is the presence of the meaning in the soul. This indicates that whoever does not find rest in Him has no heart at all, let alone intellect in his heart; rather, he is among the inanimate things. Or it indicates that every heart finds rest in Him, so whoever reports about his heart something contrary to this is a liar and an obstinate one, and whoever submits and acts in accordance with the requirement of tranquility is a believer.

Then he informed of what this oath entails, by His saying: ﴿Those who believe﴾, i.e., who brought into being the attribute of faith, ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾, i.e., as confirmation of their claim of faith, ﴿the righteous deeds﴾ (for the tranquility of their hearts in the remembrance [of Allah]). ﴿Blessed is for them﴾, i.e., goodness, pleasantness, joy, and comfort for the eye. ﴿And a good return﴾. Thus this indicated the state of the other category, as if it were said: and whoever does not find tranquility, or whose heart does not find tranquility and does not submit, [for him is] misery and an evil return.

When it was the case that in this there is a weaning from sending down the things proposed, and the aversion of those who proposed them had lasted long, and the trial with them and the patience over their harm had prolonged, the fitting thing would be for someone, whether an unbeliever or a Muslim whose patience had been strained, to say: "Are you not a messenger, to whom an answer is given as an answer was given to the messengers?" So it was said: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like the sending of the messengers, which we have already pointed to at the end of [Surah Yusuf] upon him be prayer and peace, in our saying ﴿And We did not send before you any but men to whom We revealed﴾ [Yusuf: 109], and in this surah in our saying ﴿and for every people there is a guide﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]. Like this wondrous sending, the matter is of far-reaching importance, and it is that which we have trained you upon more than once: that the return is to God, and the whole affair is in His hand, so no one else has any power over guidance or misguidance, neither by sending down a sign nor otherwise. ﴿We have sent you﴾, that is, with what We possess of greatness, ﴿to a community﴾, and it is a large group of living creatures which refers to a particular meaning peculiar to it and to no other, ﴿in which communities have already passed away﴾

Since the messengers were sent to those whom they actually embraced throughout all time, He said: ﴿before it there have passed communities﴾, whose harm to their prophets and to those who believed in them was prolonged, and who mocked them for not answering their proposals, and each community said to its prophet, out of obstinacy, after the signs had come to them: ﴿Why has no sign been sent down to him?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27], until it was as though they had agreed upon this saying. Even so, the conduct of the messengers and their followers, in their turning to supplication and their aversion from those who mock them, was the conduct of one who has despaired of any sending down. ﴿That you may recite﴾, that is, We sent you among them so that you might recite ﴿to them﴾, that is, read. Recitation (tilawa) is making the second follow the first without any interval. ﴿That which We have revealed to you﴾ from the remembrance of God, which is the greatest of signs, ﴿while they disbelieve﴾, that is, while they are in the state of disbelieving. Its recitation to them is not to be abandoned in that state, for We have a wisdom in this, even if it is hidden. We did not send you, nor the messengers before you, except to recite what is revealed, not to seek an answer to what the communities propose of signs, under the assumption that these would be a cause of someone's faith. We know best about them. All of this is consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). His saying ﴿the Most Merciful﴾ indicates the abundance of His forbearance and the length of His patience, and it portrays the ugliness of their state in facing kindness with evil and blessing with disbelief in the clearest form, while they claim to be the most thankful of people for kindness and the furthest of them from ingratitude.

Since their disbelief in the Most Merciful included their disbelief in the Qur'an and in the one to whom it was sent down, and since disbelief in the Benefactor is at the extreme of ugliness, it was as though it were said: "What then shall I do, I and those who follow me?" We do not wish for their being answered in their proposals except out of hope for their faith. Their answer concerning disbelief in what is revealed was more important, so He began with it and said: ﴿Say﴾ at that point, in faith in it: ﴿He is﴾, that is, the Most Merciful whom you have disbelieved in, ﴿my Lord﴾, who nurtures me by bringing me into being and pouring out blessings, who is good to me and to no other. I do not disbelieve His kindness as you have disbelieved it. Rather I say: ﴿there is no god but He﴾. I trust in Him in nurture, in support, and in everything else.

Since His singleness in divinity is the cause for restricting aspirations to Him, He said: ﴿In Him﴾, that is, Him alone, with no partner, ﴿I have put my trust﴾. Tawakkul (trust in God) is confidence in the management of one's affairs by referring them to God, with contentment in what He does. ﴿And to Him﴾, that is, not to anyone else, ﴿is my return﴾, that is, my place of return, in meaning by repentance and in reality by the Hereafter. This is an allusion against them, in that the reason for your disbelief is denial of the Day of Judgment.

[p. 340]

When he had finished answering the disbelief in what was revealed, the answer to disbelief in the Revelation (*waḥy*) was joined by conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) to "He is my Lord," and he said: ﴿And if﴾. This indicates that he believes about the Qur'an what it deserves, after having reported his belief about the Most Merciful (*al-Raḥmān*). That is, say: "If ﴿a Qur'an﴾ were such that by it the sensible signs came about, namely ﴿that the mountains were set in motion﴾, by even the slightest gesture from one who gestures, ﴿by it the mountains﴾, that is, removing them, despite their weight and hardness, from the face of the earth; ﴿or the earth was cut asunder﴾, that is, likewise, ﴿by it the earth﴾, despite its density, so that it split open and rivers gushed forth from it; ﴿or the dead were made to speak by it﴾, so that they heard and responded, then this Qur'an would be such, because it is a sign that has no equal. So how do they seek a sign other than it!"

Or it may be said: the implied meaning is: "If any of that had come about by a Qur'an other than this one, it would have been by it, as a delight to your eyes and a response to what you desire. But no custom has been established that any Qur'an before it would produce such things. Therefore it did not come about by this Qur'an, because God did not will that for a wisdom known to Him. No one other than God has any authority to break any of the customary patterns, neither a saint (*walī*), nor a prophet, nor anyone else, so that he would do for your sake, [by intercession - ] or by other means, something God had not willed from eternity."

﴿But﴾. It is also permissible that the implied meaning is: "If any of this were to occur at any time by a Qur'an, it would be by this Qur'an. Then, whoever memorized anything from it would be able to do whatever he wished of that: he would set in motion for himself whatever mountains he wished toward whatever lands he desired, for whatever purposes he sought; he would cut through the earth for himself rivers, gardens and other things he requested; and he would make speak whichever of the dead he wished. Then, once this door is opened, there is no difference between the power to do this and the power to do other things. So whoever memorized something from it would become capable of anything. Thereupon the wisdom of God, glorified is He, in singling out whom He wills to rescue His servants would be nullified, and this would lead to the wicked claiming, whoever wishes among them, that the matter of all this is in his hand, that he does with it whatever he wills whenever he wills. His claim, coupled with action, would then become a cause of association (*shirk*). And so that it may be known with certainty that the command is in no one's hand, rather ﴿Allah﴾, that is, the One who alone possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿has the command﴾, which is that about which one may be commanded and forbidden, ﴿entirely﴾ in this and other matters, not for me nor for any of the prophets, concerning whom you said [p. 341] that I am no less in station than they. As for the extraordinary things that occurred for them, had He not willed them they would not have occurred. So the command belongs to Him alone; whatever He wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be."

This seems to be a response to what is related in the Prophetic biography (*al-Sīra*), that the disbelievers were tempted by it. Ibn Isḥāq said: "Then Islam began to spread in Mecca among the tribes of Quraysh, among men and women. Their nobles gathered and sent to him (ﷺ), and they spoke with him about refraining from them, and offered to make him their king and other things. He refused and said: 'Indeed God has sent me to you as a messenger, and has sent down to me a Book, and has commanded me to be for you a bearer of good news and a warner.' They said: 'You know that there is no one among people with a narrower land, less water or harder life than us. So ask your Lord who sent you with what He sent you with, to move these mountains away from us, which have hemmed us in, and to spread out our land for us, and to cause rivers to gush forth in it like the rivers of Syria and Iraq.' " Al-Baghawī added: "'For you are not, as you claim, less favored by your Lord than David, to whom He subjected the mountains to glorify with him, or than Solomon, for whom He subjected the wind, so that we could ride it to Syria for our provisions and return in one day.' " [Back to Ibn Isḥāq:] "'And let him raise for us those of our forefathers who have passed away, and let Quṣayy ibn Kilāb be among those raised for us, for he was a truthful elder. We shall ask them about what you say: is it true or false? If they confirm you, and you do what we have asked, we shall believe you, and we shall know thereby your station with God, and that He sent you to us as a messenger, as you claim.' " Al-Baghawī added: "'For Jesus used to give life to the dead, and you are no less in station with your Lord than he.'" Their request thus implied that their claim, that his claim to have the Qur'an sent down is not valid unless he does these things.

When all this was a despair of anyone's faith being attained through what they proposed, the denunciation followed upon whoever was not benefited by that. So God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have those who believe not despaired﴾, with the causal particle *fa* (so), ﴿of the faith of those who proposed the signs in what they proposed, knowing﴾ ﴿that﴾, that is, that ﴿if Allah willed﴾, that is, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, to guide every person by a will coinciding with His existence, ﴿He would have guided all people﴾. He clarified that the *lām* is for comprehensiveness (*istighrāq*) by His saying: ﴿all together﴾, that is, with the easiest will. Knowledge of a thing necessitates despair of its opposite, [p. 342] but He did not guide them all, so He did not will that. What He wills alone comes to be, so a group among them will continue to be disbelievers. It is clear that ﴿yaʾyas﴾ is used in its proper sense (*ʿalā bābihā*). Likewise, in the verse they cited as evidence that it means "to know" (*ʿalima*), its meaning could be: "Did you not despair of my harm or of my killing, knowing that I am the son of the knight Zahdam, so that my vengeance will not be lost?" Likewise is the reading of ʿAlī and those companions with him, may God be pleased with them all: "Have not those who believe become clear..." That is, the people of misguidance do not believe in any of the signs, knowing that the command belongs entirely to God, and that their faith is not contingent on anything other than His will.

Since it was known from this that some of them would not believe, the hearts of the believers were constricted [p. 343] because of this, as they witnessed the harm inflicted by the disbelievers. So He followed it with what would console them, linking it by conjunction to what He had decreed as the result of the absence of His will. He said: ﴿And calamity will not cease to strike those who disbelieved﴾, that is, who covered the light of their intellects, ﴿for what they have done﴾, that is, for the evil to which they have become accustomed until it became their nature, ﴿a catastrophe﴾, that is, a calamity that disturbs them with vengeance from His might, through the hand of whomever He wills. It is from the striking with a whip (*miqraʿa*). ﴿Or it will descend﴾, that is, that catastrophe will descend a second time, ﴿close to their dwelling﴾, so that it weakens their affairs, ﴿until the promise of Allah comes﴾, that is, the promise of the Supreme King, either the conquest of Mecca or victory over all the disbelievers in the time of Jesus, peace be upon him, whereupon it will cease, because He does not leave a single disbeliever on earth. At other times, such as the time of the conquest of noble Mecca, the meaning would be specific to some. ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, that is, the One possessing all perfection, ﴿does not break His promise﴾, that is, His pledge, neither its time nor its place. A promise (*waʿd*) is the binding of news with the inclusion of benefit; a threat (*waʿīd*) is binding it with rebuke and harm; and breaking (*ikhlāf*) is the violation of what news contained, whether of good or of evil.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 32:

When the answer concerning their disbelief in what was revealed (al-muhi) and in what He revealed to him, and concerning how closely they clung to it, was complete, He followed that with consolation for the one to whom it was revealed, ﷺ. This is because what prompted them to demand a distinct response in the form of the proposed signs (al-ayat al-muqtarahat) was the mockery of the disbelievers. So He said: ﴿And messengers were certainly mocked﴾, meaning, by the lowest of creation and others, ﴿before you﴾.

Since sending messengers did not cover all times, let alone mockery, He introduced the preposition, saying ﴿before you﴾, because they did not bring the proposed signs. "Istihza'" (mockery) means seeking ridicule (al-huzu'), which is making something apparent, the opposite of concealing it, for the purpose of belittling. ﴿Then I gave respite﴾, meaning, as a consequence of their mockery, I gave respite (amlaytu) ﴿to those who disbelieved﴾, meaning, I granted them time in ease and abundance, like the beast that is given respite, that is, it is allowed to graze and extend itself. I did not make this a cause for answering them in what they proposed, nor for hastening their punishment, as a narrow-minded and shrewd person would do. ﴿Then﴾ ("thumma") after a long period of respite, ﴿I seized them﴾, meaning with a seizure of subjugation and retribution. ﴿Then how﴾, meaning, my seizing of them was a cause for asking whoever was slow to accept our messengers, or who suspected us of neglecting them: it is said to him, "How ﴿was My punishment﴾"? This is an interrogative whose meaning is amazement at what befell the deniers, and affirmation. Within it is a severe warning.

[p. 347] When what has been established, through what preceded of His power over reward and punishment, His lowering the earth, His raising the heavens, and His setting up the signs by means of the manifest clear proofs, is that no one other than Him has any command whatsoever, and it is confirmed that everyone is in His grip, there follows from this the statement: ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul for what it has earned﴾. Since standing (al-qiyam) indicates dominance (al-isti'la'), He clarified it by His words: ﴿over every soul﴾, that is, every righteous soul and others, ﴿for what it has earned﴾, meaning He does with them what He wills, by granting respite, seizing them, and other things. [Is He] like one who is not so, like their partners, which have no standing over anything at all?

Since the answer is certain, namely: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾, it is as if it were said, in amazement at this question: Who is it that imagined that He has a likeness? It is said: ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾ in Him, ﴿and set up for Allah﴾, that is, for the Supreme King, ﴿partners﴾. It is permissible to take "min" (from) as introducing a predicate with the meaning: "they did not declare Him One," and to join ﴿and set up﴾ to it, so that it is as if it were said: What, then, does He do to them? It is said: ﴿Say: Name them﴾ by their true names. For when they are named, and you know their realities, that they are stones or something else of that kind which is the seat of incapacity and the locus of poverty, one knows the folly of their minds and the feebleness of their opinions. Then say to them: Have you turned back from this to acknowledging that they are among His servants? ﴿Or will you inform Him﴾, that is, tell Him with a great informing, ﴿of what He knows not﴾, while His knowledge encompasses everything, ﴿in the earth﴾, regarding their being gods, by a decisive proof.

[p. 348] ﴿Or of an outward saying﴾, that is, by a persuasive argument uttered by the mouth. Whatever He does not know is not a thing. This is close to what came earlier in His words: ﴿Or have they set up for Allah partners who created as He creates?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16], in that if it were so, there would be some manifest likeness to Him in it. These modes of expression proclaim the incapacity of creation and loudly declare that it is not the speech of creatures.

Since the implied meaning is: they have no decisive proof for any of that, nor any manifest saying, He built upon it His words: ﴿Rather, their scheming has been made attractive﴾, that is, the making attractive has occurred by the command of One whose command is not turned back, at the hand of one who was ﴿to those who disbelieved﴾, that is, for them. He expressed it thus to draw attention to the attribute which led them down to the belief in falsehood, namely concealing what the proof of reason, supported by the evidence of transmitted text, had led to. ﴿Their scheming﴾, that is, their affair, by which they intended what is intended by scheming, namely showing one thing and concealing another. This is because they displayed that their partners were truly gods, while they knew the falsity of that; inwardly they had nothing but the imitation of their fathers. And they displayed that they worship them so that they may draw near to Allah in nearness and that they may intercede for them. Or they altered the face of truth by what they deceived [p. 349] [the weak] with, and the situation extended with them until they believed it to be true.

The root m-k-r, in whatever order it occurs: makara, rakama, ramaka, karama, kamara, revolves around covering and concealment. Thus al-makr is deception. They said: it is the scheming by what does not appear; when it appears it is kayd. It necessarily involves striving to gather scattered matters to conceal what is intended. From the sense of gathering comes al-makr, which is the fine fullness of the calf of the leg, that is, its plumpness, and this necessarily involves the bodily fertility and bounty. From it also is al-makr, a kind of plant, its singular being makrah, named so because of its being well watered. Abu Hanifa said: al-makr is among the herbage of the summer heat, a grey plant with no leaves, which grows in plain and sand. It seems to be compared to a leg for its lack of leaves, or because of its greyness and its bareness, like something covered. Al-makr is also a reddish clay that resembles ochre; it seems to have been named so for the turbidity in it. And al-mikarrah of dates is the one that is not moist but has some softness in it; it seems to have been named so because its colour then begins to become turbid. Al-rukam is placing one thing upon another, so it is markum and rukam. The piling up of a thing, when some of it becomes dense upon other parts, is a cause of concealment. [p. 350] Al-rukmah is gathered clay, and likewise gathered dust. And it is said: "wa jazza 'an marratikum al-tariq", meaning the highway, because its dust becomes compacted and firmly packed. Al-ramak and al-rumkah, with a dammah, are among the colours of camels; it is darker than the leaf-colour, a colour whose greyness is mixed with blackness, so it is armak, because it is a cause of the hiding of what is in it. From it derives al-raamik, which is mixtures blended with musk to make it a perfume. Ramaka al-rajul bi-l-maqam means when the man stayed in the place, because he covers it with himself and his goods while he himself is concealed in it. Armakat ghayri means when she made me stay in a place where I resided. Al-ramakah is the female of the barādhīn (a breed of horses), a Persian word arabized, because it conceals the nobility of the Arab when it gives birth to him. Ramkan is a well-known place, a definite name. It is said: ramaka al-rajul when he became thin and what was in his hand went away, so he was concealed from view or became hidden after being well known in his good state. Ramaktu al-bazi wa al-saqr tarmikan means when I pointed to it with a bird, because you removed the veil from it. Al-yarmuk is a place with great flame that covers what is in it. Al-karim is the opposite of al-la'im, and that is the miser, the one of base spirit and low lineage. When someone is niggardly and these qualities are not gathered in him, it is said of him: "bakhil" (miserly), and it is not said "la'im" (base). So al-karim is one who conceals the vices of character by displaying their virtues. And takarrama means when he kept himself far from baseness and raised himself above it. The root of karam in the language is excellence and elevation. When they say: so-and-so is karim, they only mean elevated and virtuous, so karam necessarily involves concealing faults. Allah is al-Karim, that is, the excellent, the elevated, so said some of the people of language. It is said: He who pardons sins. It is said: He who does not reproach when He gives. When they say: so-and-so is the most noble of his people, they only mean: the highest in rank and most excellent in standing. All of this necessarily involves generosity and the concealing of faults. From this it is said: a karim horse, and a karimah tree, when it is higher than its counterparts and more excellent.

﴿Indeed, there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾ [al-Naml: 29], that is, elevated and honourable. It seems that here it is applied to that which contains mere excellence, by likening it to the karim in one aspect of meaning. Kāramtu al-rajul means each of us did toward his companion what generosity requires. Al-karm is the grape-vine, and nothing else is named with it. Al-kurum are necklaces that women make, like the collars, because they indicate the rank of their wearer. Al-karamah is a tray placed over the head of a flask of grain, because it is its cover, and only what has excellence is covered. From it they say: "laka al-hubb wa al-karamah" (to you, the love and the honour). Al-karam is the short one among [p. 352] men, as if he were compared to the grain-tray. Al-kamarah, with the vowel-harakat, is the tip of a human's penis specifically, named so because the foreskin covers it. Rajul makmur means when the circumciser has cut his kumrah. Takamara al-rajulan means when two men boast with their members, comparing which is greater in kumrah. Al-kumri is fresh dates not moistened on their tree, but fallen unripe and then moistened in the earth; it seems to have been named so because it is more turbid than what is moistened on the tree, and it also resembles the kumrah in its formation. Al-kamri from Ibn Duraid is the short man; it seems he was likened to the moist date. Others said it is also the name of a place.

When He mentioned the making attractive of their scheming, He followed it with the indication of it, saying: ﴿And they were turned away﴾, that is, they clung to what had been made attractive to them, or they schemed with it until they went astray in themselves and turned others away ﴿from the way﴾, which is not called "way" for anything other than it, namely the straight one. For what is other than it is crookedness, bewilderment and confusion, which is nothing; rather nothing is better than it. So they did not travel the way, nor did they leave others to travel it; so they went astray and led others astray. This is no wonder, for Allah led them astray. ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray﴾, that is, He to whom the whole affair belongs, by His will to make them stray, ﴿for him there is no guide﴾.

Then it is as if it were said: "What then is for them in return for what they did of that?" So it is said: (p-353) ﴿For them﴾, that is, those who disbelieved, ﴿is a punishment﴾, which is continuous pain; and from it comes "al-'adhb" (sweet water), because it persists in the throat. ﴿In the life of this world﴾ is hardship, through the resistance of the party of Allah against them in their barring [others] from the path, [and] what is connected with that of killing and captivity. And for them in the Hereafter, if they die upon that, is a punishment. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾, that is, more severe in hardship, which is the severity of the matter upon the soul, to the point that the heart nearly breaks. ﴿And they have no protector from Allah﴾, that is, the Greatest King, ﴿against any [harm]﴾, that is, no preventer who would prevent them if He intends evil for them, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. Al-waqi is the agent noun of al-wiqaya (protection), which is the shield that repels harm.

(p-354) When He had threatened them for their neglect regarding the right of God, the soul yearned for what awaits their opposites. It was as if it were said: "What is there for those who opposed them for God's sake?" So it was answered: "The Garden." It was as if it were then said: "And what is it?" So it was answered: "Truly, it is in its majesty, the loftiness of its beauty, and the nobility of its qualities, which are exalted beyond attainment, and can only be conveyed through the striking of parables." It was then asked: "What is its likeness?" So it was answered: ﴿The likeness of the Garden which﴾. Since the intended meaning is the realization of the true promise, especially as it is known that the one who promises is God, He used the passive form in His saying: ﴿has been promised to the God-fearing﴾. The predicate is omitted, and its estimated form is: "What I relate to you is that it is gardens: palaces and trees." (p-354)

Al-Zajjaj said: The predicate is "a garden," described by what is mentioned, so that it would be a likeness for what is hidden from us through what we observe. ﴿Beneath it flow﴾. Since, if flowing water were to cover it entirely, it would be a sea and not gardens, He introduced the preposition to indicate that it applies only to some of its lands. So He said: ﴿from beneath it﴾, that is, beneath its palaces and trees, ﴿the rivers﴾. It was also said that this mentioned phrase is itself the predicate, just as you say: "The description of Zayd is 'tall and dark'."

Since this is true irrigation in a land that is in the utmost purity and goodness, it was the cause of the lasting of its fruit and the steadfastness of its foliage. Therefore He followed it with His saying: ﴿Its food﴾, that is, its fruit which is eaten, ﴿is everlasting﴾, never ceasing ever, ﴿and its shade﴾ is not as it is in this world; it is not erased by the sun or anything else. Abu Hayyan said: One says "mathalta al-shay'" when one describes a thing and brings it close to understanding; this is not a striking of a parable. It is like His saying: ﴿To God belongs the highest likeness﴾ [al-Nahl: 60], meaning the highest attribute. Thus he said. It is possible, however, that this is literal, and there is an omitted element, which is: a garden among the gardens of this world, beneath which rivers flow, and so on to the end; and this is from the saying of al-Zajjaj.

Then He began another statement, to magnify its matter and glorify its affair, in His saying, the Exalted:

(p-355) ﴿That﴾, that is, the Garden of lofty attributes, ﴿is the final outcome of those who were God-fearing﴾. Then He repeated the threat against the disbelievers, saying: ﴿And the final outcome of the disbelievers﴾, that is, the ultimate end of the affair of those ﴿who disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾, which includes disbelief [in the revelation (bil-wahy)] and in the One to whom it was revealed, ﴿is the Fire﴾.

When He had described the two groups, that the revelation sent down to you is the truth, by the soundness of their intellects and the genuineness of their response, which leads to righteousness and brings about every happiness, and the disbelievers in it, by the weakness of their intellects, which drives them to corruption and leads to an evil end, and (the surah) had gone on in what suits this until it closed with the same kind of closing that it closed with that, He followed that with His saying (and it is possible that its connection to what came before is that it is coordinated with an omitted clause which is the cause of the closing of the previous verse; its implied meaning being: because what was sent down to him displeased them, out of envy and ignorance):

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾, that is, by the greatness We possess, which rescued them from error, ﴿the Book﴾, and they did not disbelieve in the Most Merciful, nor in what was sent down, nor in the one who was sent, ﴿rejoice at what﴾. Since the thing sent down indicates, by its miraculous nature, the one who sent it down, He used the passive form in His saying: ﴿has been sent down to you﴾, that is, from this greatest Book, because it agrees with those earlier Books, for the speech of God is all from one niche (of lamps). Their being singled out is because they are the ones who benefit from the Book rather than others, so it is as if it had been sent down only to them. This coordination (p-356) suggests that the relative pronoun there is in the nominative, as the subject of a nominal sentence. ﴿And among the factions﴾, from the people of idols and the Scripture-people who formed factions against the Messenger of God (ﷺ), ﴿is one who denies part of it﴾, such as monotheism, the description of Islam, the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), and what follows from that, of what they had distorted and altered, and who wants the matter to follow his aim in it. So the polytheists wanted the revelation to praise their gods in some verses, or to drop the mention of their defects. The Jews wanted what agrees with the branches of the Torah to be sent down, just as what agreed with the foundations was sent down, and they denied abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of one ruling by a later one). The People of the Gospel wanted what they desired about the Messiah to be sent down, and similar things. The exegetes said: they did not deny the narratives, some of the rulings, and the parables that are established in their books and not distorted. So, because of their disbelief in that part, He commanded him to inform them of his belief, whether they disbelieved or were thankful, and He said:

﴿Say: I have only been commanded﴾, that is, a firm command has been issued, about which there is no doubt and no change, by the One to whom all command belongs, ﴿to worship God﴾, that is, the One to whom nothing is like, ﴿alone﴾, and for this reason He said: ﴿and not to associate anything with Him﴾. I do only what He commands me, without regard to anything else. My religion is confined to what you have denied. ﴿To Him﴾ alone ﴿I call﴾, and ﴿to Him﴾ alone is ﴿my return﴾, that is, my return, its place and its time, meaningfully by repentance when one slackens in carrying out His right, and concretely by resurrection for recompense. The Book (kitāb) is the page in which there is writing (khatt), which is the act of writing, namely the composition of letters that are read on the page. Joy (farah) is the pleasure of the heart which dispels distress by attaining what is desired. A faction (hizb) is a group that rises to meet a calamity.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 13, verse 37:

When these verses had made clear the degrees of inimitability (i'jaz) that they made clear, Allah the Exalted followed the mention of what He had sent down with His saying: ﴿And thus﴾, meaning: and like this sending down, unique in its example and far-reaching in its attainment. It is not far-fetched that it is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon ﴿Thus We have sent you﴾ [al-Ra'd: 30], or like the sending down of the books of the People of the Scripture. ﴿We have sent it down﴾, by what We possess of greatness, as ﴿a judgment in Arabic﴾, meaning filled with wisdom that decides by the truth, surpassing all books in this description. And ḥukm (judgment): the decisive determination of meaning according to what wisdom calls for; it is also the separation of the matter upon the truth. So the meaning is that no one is able to annul any part of it, for that in reality is ḥukm, and whatever is not like that is not ḥukm. And ʿarabī (Arabic): that which proceeds according to the ways of the Arabs in their speech. So do not turn toward what their desires call you to, so that they propose it, such as supporting you with a kingdom, or bestowing upon you a treasure, or leaving some of what is revealed to you concerning the faults of their gods, the foolishness of their minds, (p-358) the misguidance of their fathers, or other of their demands which, if I brought them to them, they would not have believed, unless Allah wills. This is regarding the worshippers of idols, and likewise regarding the People of the Scripture in what they call to of returning to their qibla and the like. ﴿And if you follow their desires﴾ in any part of that, from abrogation (naskh) or other matters, in the qibla or other than it, and especially regarding what they ask of the proposed signs, as the Exalted said: ﴿And if you brought those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qibla, and you are not a follower of their qibla, and some of them are not followers of the qibla of others. And if you followed their desires﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145], the verse.

Since the intended meaning is generality in time, He removed the preposition and brought ﴿mā﴾, because it is more general than ﴿alladhī﴾ and more indefinite, so it is the hidden in meaning, which fits the context of revelation, which is unseen, and its meaning is obscure, except for some individuals, among the ignorant, unlike the first verse of al-Baqarah, for it concerns the Abrahamic religion, which is perceived by the light of reason arising from the examination of sensible things. So He said: ﴿after what has come to you﴾. And since He had bestowed upon him ﷺ things other than knowledge, He clarified the intended meaning of His saying: ﴿of the knowledge﴾, meaning by revelation, that such following does not avail them, whether that following was in the roots of the Shari'ah or its branches, whether hidden or manifest.

(p-359) And since what is conditioned is the encompassing of the entire span of time with the following of desires, He said: ﴿you would have then﴾ at that time ﴿from Allah﴾, meaning the Supreme King, and He intensified the negation, so He said: ﴿any protector﴾, meaning a helper who takes charge of whoever aids you and all your affairs, as a near relative takes charge of his near relative. And since the signification of ﴿mā﴾ is more general than the signification of ﴿alladhī﴾, as it includes the apparent and the hidden, and whoever opposes the hidden is more excusable than whoever opposes the apparent, He negated the more specific of the helpers, so He said: ﴿nor any defender﴾, meaning one who shields you by himself, placing himself before you. Some of the helpers may exist who do not hear of this, and this is an incitement to the community and an exhortation to steadfastness in the religion and firmness in it. And hawā (desire), with a short vowel: the inclination of natures toward a thing by appetite; and ʿilm (knowledge): the clarification of a thing as it truly is.

(p-٣٦٠) When hopes of their accepting his message were cut off, whether the hope of their following him or the fear of their refusing him, and when some of them had said, "If he were a prophet, his prophethood would have kept him busy and away from marrying many women," the matter called for information about what had been the case for the Messengers in similar circumstances. So God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We certainly sent messengers﴾, meaning with Our majesty, ﴿messengers﴾. Since the times of the Messengers were not general to all time, He introduced the preposition and said: ﴿before you﴾, meaning, and We did not make them angels, but made them human beings. "And" We burdened their backs with what calls for (p-360) tolerance and peaceful dealings, by pleasing their nations in some of their desires, or by settling the matter when hostility was certain, by carrying out the threat. "We made" for them, meaning by Our greatness, ﴿wives﴾, meaning women whom they married. The zawj (spouse) is the companion, male or female, and here it means the female. "And offspring" (dhurriyyah), which is a group scattered by birth from one father in general. Their peoples did to them what is done to you of mockery. So none of them followed any of the desires of his nation. "And" We did not place in their hands the bringing of what the obstinate ones propose of signs, lest it destroy them.
